['Mr. Speaker, yesterday on the orders of the day the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) asked for certain information with regard to a supplementary trade agreement recently concluded with France, and I promised to make a statement to-day. It is very brief. I might perhaps in fairness say, first, that the original negotiations were initiated by the former administration and concluded by the present one.
An exchange of notes between Canada and France was effected at Paris on March 20, 1936, whereby each country accorded to the other some concessions additional to those provided for under the trade agreement of May 12, 1933, and the additional protocol of February 26, 1935. The new arrangement came into force yesterday, March 31, 1936. The Canadian government agreed to make, by order in council, the following adjustments in favour of France.
Item 156(a)

Rum-intermediate tariff less a discount of 30 per cent.
Item ex 197 and ex 198-Cigarette paper, gummed or not, in rolls-intermediate tariff on item No. 197 less a discount of 30 per cent.
Item ex 199-Cigarette paper, gummed or not. in tubes, booklets or packets-intermediate tariff less 30 per cent.
In return the French government gives to Canada the minimum tariff of France on a number of commodities, including selenium, knitting machine needles, outboard motors and hairpins. I might say that the department has received numerous requests from Canadian exporters of these products who stated they could do business with France if they were given the benefit of the minimum tariff of that country.
In addition, France has agreed to continue quotas on porcelain insulators, electric heating apparatus and vacuum cleaners, which were enumerated in schedule F of the additional protocol of February 26, 1935. In the exchange of notes France also undertakes to grant Canada sympathetic treatment with respect to quotas generally. I might add that the further details were published in the edition of March 2S of the Commercial Intelligence Journal, of which every hon. member received a copy.']

speechtext:
Before the orders of the day are proceeded with, I was proposing to ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) whether he has any statement to make in connection with the Alberta situation. I assume that probably he would do so in any event without being asked.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance): As my right hon. friend has anticipated, the government deems it right to give the house immediate and full advice with respect to the Alberta situation. I do not think that advice can be given in any better way than by reading the correspondence between the premier and the provincial treasurer of Alberta and myself as representing the government of Canada.
The first communication is in the form of a letter from Edmonton dated March 12, 1936, signed by C. Cockroft, provincial treasurer of Alberta:
Edmonton, March 12, 1936. Dear Mr. Dunning,
I regret very much that I am obliged to approach you again on a matter which is, I am sure, of as much concern to yourself as it is to me. It should hardly be necessary for me to remind you that there is a debenture issue of $3,200,000 falling due on April 1. I dislike very much making this approach, but the issues are so vital that I thought I had better communicate with you and let you know how far I could go in regard to this maturity.
We have in the sinking fund available on this issue, $354,000, and in addition we can add to this figure $196,000, making a total of $550,000; the balance to be met of $2,650,000, we wish you would advance to us on the same terms and conditions as applied to our January 15 maturity.
I sent you the 1936-37 provincial budget, which I doubt if you have had time to peruse. You will note, however, that we have provided for a substantial increase in revenue by additional taxation. Changing the procedure which has been followed in past years, we have dealt with unemployment relief as a current income expenditure. In view of its continuing character we feel that this procedure is sound and if our increased estimated revenue is realized and no unforeseen expenditures of any magnitude have to be met, we will be in a position to finance our share of the direct relief estimated.
Taking the budget as a whole, every effort has been put forth by this government to meet its difficult financial situation and if our
16S4
Alberta Financial Situation

expectations are realized, we should not be obliged later on to approach your government or to raise funds in any other manner to meet the expenditures of unemployment relief, as this government has done in past years.
I sincerely trust that you will see your way clear to assist us in this matter and would appreciate it if you will let the writer know, preferably by wire, whether you would desire to go into this matter in more detail, in which event I will arrange to be in Ottawa a few days before the end of this month. It would of course be a convenience if arrangements could be made by wire, as our legislature is in session and as you know the treasurer is at the beck and call of all and sundry.
With best regards.
Yours sincerely,
C. Cockroft, Provincial Treasurer.
Next is a telegram dated March 17, signed
by myself:
C. Cockroft Provincial Treasurer Edmonton, Alberta
Ottawa, Ontario,
March 17, 1936.
Your letter requesting dominion loan to assist you in meeting April first maturity reached me simultaneously with premier's newspaper announcement that province was about to introduce legislation reducing interest rates on outstanding debt apparently without reference to proposed loan council arrangement. Announcement has already had serious adverse effect on market particularly for western provincial bonds and proposal if carried out would nullify all efforts already made and proposed to be made by dominion to protect credit of the provinces and the dominion as a whole. In view of action contemplated by province I do not see how I could justify to parliament and the country the loan for which you are now asking.
Chas. A. Dunning.
Then, on March 19, I telegraphed to the premier of Alberta and also to the premiers of the other three western provinces, saying:
Ottawa,
March 19, 1936.
Hon. Wm. Aberhart Premier of Alberta Edmonton, Alberta.
As you know authority to make loans or give guarantees to provinces will expire March thirty-first. It is not the intention to ask parliament for authority to give assistance in future in respect of maturing obligations or for general provincial purposes. Proposed constitutional amendment implies virtually unanimous approval of provinces. As objections have been raised by some provinces and as difficulties may arise in connection with early maturities we wish the provinces particularly interested to be fully cognizant of dominion's attitude and future policy. Believe matter sufficiently important for conference with premiers or provincial treasurers of four western provinces. Would it be possible for you to attend such a conference to be held next week.
Chas. A. Dunning.
It will be remembered that in the letter from the provincial treasurer which I read

first he spoke of coming to Ottawa, and the dominion government thought the situation sufficiently serious to ask if it were possible to secure a further conference of the premiers or treasurers, of the four provinces particularly interested. In that connection I may say that it was found rather difficult, from the point of view of the premiers and the treasurers of the provinces to arrange for such a conference, because of the fact that their legislatures were in session.
Replying to the telegram I have just read was a telegram from the premier of Alberta to myself, dated March 20:
Edmonton, Alta.,
March 20, 1936.
Hon. Charles A. Dunning,
Minister of Finance, [DOT]	.
Ottawa, Ont.
Impossible financially to meet our obligation April first. Alberta legislature will not complete its session until next week. Urge that arrangements be made by federal government for this maturity and will confer at your convenience afterwards.
William Aberhart.
I then wired on March 20, to Hon. William Aberhart, premier of Alberta, as follows:
Ottawa, March 20, 1936. Hon. William Aberhart,
Premier of Alberta,
Edmonton, Alta.
Your wire to-day's date. For past five months dominion has been making utmost effort to work out with provinces solution for financial difficulties of certain provinces. At dominion-provincial conference and subsequent meetings of financial committee it was made abundantly clear that the dominion cannot consider making further loans for the purpose of meeting provincial maturities and cannot possibly consent to any plan which removed from dominion parliament absolute control at all times of extent to which dominion guarantees or loans shall be given. In these conferences we evolved a plan whereby provinces finding it impossible to meet existing obligations could obtain privilege of dominion guarantee for refunding and new borrowing under a loan council arrangement. With unanimous consent of representatives of all provinces dominion undertook to initiate steps to secure necessary enabling powers and after submitting proposed draft to all provinces requisite legislation has now been introduced in parliament. In January we agreed to assist you in meeting a provincial maturity because we felt that you had not at that time had sufficient time to consider fully the nature of the proposed arrangement. As over two months have since elapsed that reason no longer applies. It is unreasonable to assume that with a maturity coming on April first the Alberta government has not been giving careful consideration to the problem thereby created. Yet apart from various newspaper statements reported to have been made by you we have not been made aware of your attitude to the proposed loan council arrangement under which dominion guarantee would be available to the province. It may be that the views of the dominion and

16S5
Alberta Financial Situation
Alberta cannot be reconciled but my telegram of yesterday was intended to invite a final effort to avert serious impairment of the credit of Alberta and other western provinces which default on your impending maturity would inevitably cause. Regret impossible for me to suggest any other course.
Chas. A. Dunning.
On March 21. I received this reply from the premier of Alberta:
Edmonton, Alta., via Ottawa, Ont.,
March 21, 7.30 p.m.
Hon. Chas. A. Dunning,
30 Whitney avenue,
Toronto, Ont.
Quite appreciate sincerity of statements in your wire. Replying categorically. Agree dominion has made utmost effort for last five months. Dominion parliament certainly has right to absolute control of extent of guarantees and loans to provinces. ' Agree conferences discussed plan regarding refunding existing obligations with dominion guarantee. In this regard Alberta was the first to agree to earmark certain revenues against interest upon refunded debt in accordance with federal bill drafted March fourth section three subsection one clause A B C. Appreciate your assistance in meeting January maturity. Reference lapse two months we have given consideration during this period but obviously impossible to arrive at definite conclusion for reason see section one proposed bill that parliament of Canada has not defined the terms and conditions to be prescribed by it. We are not evading this point but no matter what the requirements might be you could hardly expect advanced definite commitment by any legislature on undetermined details. Failure to advise regarding loan council is explained in preceding paragraph. We sincerely hope that the views of Alberta and the dominion can be reconciled. We appreciate your invitation and would have gladly accepted but introduction of taxation bills and other important acts incident to our budget made it imperative for provincial treasurer and self to remain here until close of session. As evidenced by her budget Alberta is doing everything possible to meet her obligations with the one objective of ceasing to be a financial burden on the dominion. Trust you and your colleagues will give immediate and most serious consideration to the drafting of the importing provisions of the loan council which will insure approval by our legislature.
William Aberhart.
On March 23, I replied as follows:
Ottawa, Ontario, March 23, 1936.
Hon. Wm. Aberhart Premier of Alberta Edmonton, Alta.
Your Saturday's wire. Am glad that you appreciate efforts made by dominion during past five months to meet financial difficulties of certain provinces and also dominion's right to absolute control of extent of guarantees and loans to provinces. I do not understand your statement that dominion has not defined the terms and conditions to be prescribed by it under loan council arrangement. In meetings of committee on financial questions in which your provincial treasurer took part these terms
and conditions were fully considered and the minutes of the committee sent to all provinces describe them in all essential detail. Moreover the draft of the British North America Act amendment bill which you have seen covers fully in legal form nature of the security to be given by province for dominion's security. The only points that remain to be covered in legal phraseology are the constitution and powers of the individual loan councils but the minutes referred to above should leave no doubt about these points. In brief a council consisting of representative named by the province and the dominion Minister of Finance with the Bank of Canada governor acting as technical adviser will have power to approve any program for refunding of existing provincial debt and any future borrowing by provinces before dominion guarantee will be given. This is the sum and substance of the matter and I cannot conceive that there would be any controversy over details. Am glad to note that you hope the views of Alberta and dominion can be reconciled but only a week remains for such reconciliation and as stated in my previous wires my request for a conference this week was to enable such reconciliation to be made in sufficient time.
Chas. A. Dunning.
On the same day a communication similar to the following was sent to all four western premiers:
Ottawa, March 23, 1936. Honourable William Aberhart,
Premier of Alberta,
Edmonton, Alberta.
The dominion government to-day were strongly of the view that it would not be advisable to go forward with constitutional amendment bill resolution for which is now on the order paper if any of the provinces object to its being proceeded with. Would you therefore please advise nie at earliest possible moment whether you object to our proceeding further with the legislation designed to implement decisions of the committee on financial questions and to make it possible for any province desiring to participate in loan council arrangement to obtain dominion guarantee for refunding purposes.
Charles A. Dunning.
On March 24, the following wire was received from Mr. Aberhart:
1936 March 24, 6.56 p.m. Edmonton, Alta., March 24, 4.37 p.m.
Hon. Charles A. Dunning Minister of Finance, Ottawa, Ont.
Will reply fully to your wires to-morrow.
William Aberhart,
Premier.
And on March 25 there is the following wire from Mr. Aberhart to myself:
Edmonton, Alta., March 25, 1936.
Hon. Chas. A. Dunning Minister of Finance, Ottawa, Ont.
Your wire twenty-third. Reference minutes provincial treasurers meetings we consider conditions outlined inapplicable to assistance by dominion which does not extend to entire funded indebtedness of province. Only refer to this in substantiation of position we took in our
Alberta Financial Situation

Saturdays wire. We have reviewed our complete situation and taking everything into consideration we are drafting legislation along following lines in which we hope you will concur and cooperate. We have in mind fixing an early date for the maturity of outstanding bonds bearing interest at five, five and half and six per cent and issuing approximately sixty-seven million dollars provincial perpetual stock interest three per cent for purpose of retiring in cash or by exchange equal total of mentioned bonds and also including all of the maturities for five or six years so that we would have no early maturities to provide for.
It is not our intention to include presently outstanding Alberta government stock. We would however include all our savings certificates. To insure due payment of interest on stock our dominion subsidies would be charged with the payment of the interest. This plan means that the dominion would incur no liability for the principal and would be fully protected for interest by the hypothecation of subsidies. The saving resulted from the above plus sinking fund included in our budge would on a cash basis about balance our total budget. May we reiterate request for your assistance in meeting maturity due April first to extent two million six hundred and fifty thousand dollars, we providing balance. Proposed bill provides first guarantee by Canada payment principal and/or interest and/or sinking fund in respect of present and/or future securities; second empowering lieutenant governor in council create an issue perpetual provincial stock paying three per cent interest; third hypothecating subsidy; fourth accelerating maturity date existing bonds holder accepting stock in exchange in full satisfaction; fifth to accept lawful money of Canada in full satisfaction sixth act to come into force by proclamation.
William Aberhart.
To that I replied on March 26, as follows:
Department of Finance, Ottawa, March 26, 1936. Honourable William Aberhart,
Premier of Alberta,
Edmonton, Alberta.
Your wire twenty-fifth. Do not understand your reference to minutes provincial treasurers meetings. It was fully understood that any province desiring to participate in loan council scheme could with loan council approval refund entire existing indebtedness under dominion guarantee also that if any province did not desire to refund existing debt but wished to take advantage of loan council arrangement for future borrowing this privilege would also be available under similar conditions. You outline a refunding program which any province participating in loan council would be entitled to submit but such suggested program which necessarily involves highly technical matters would naturally be one for detailed analysis and working out with the expert assistance available through loan council. Your program does not contemplate what would be position with respect to further borrowings for necessary capital purposes. Necessity for providing means of dealing with future borrowings is obvious otherwise dominion would be unable to effectively control from time to time extent to which its own credit would be pledged. Would also point out that I know of no existing constitu-
[Mr. Dunning.l	*^-1
tional authority under which dominion subsidies could be pledged as provided in your proposal. Arrangements under which loans will be made to your province or guarantees given to enable you to refund existing debt have already been repeatedly made clear to you. You have not answered my question as to whether you object to our proceeding further with legislation designed to implement decisions of committee on financial questions.
Charles A. Dunning.
On March 27, 1936, the following telegram from Mr. Aberhart, was addressed to myself:
Hon. C. A. Dunning, Minister of Finance, Ottawa, Ont.
Edmonton, Alta.,
March 27, 1936.
Reference your wire twenty-sixth we have no objection dominion government proceeding with constitutional amendment bill. Reference our request for assistance to meet maturity April first we still feel we cannot agree to future loan council regulations controlling future borrowings for a refunding advance of this character. Beyond recent advance we expect to go through the coming season without asking the dominion to assist further agricultural relief. Beyond nominal capital expenditures provided in budget we have no additional ones in contemplation. Taking up maturities for some years to come with new stock issue as covered in recent wire the dominion's assistance should not be required beyond the maturity now under discussion. In view of no existing constitutional authority to hypothecate subsidy we request dominion to agree to guarantee interest only on proposed stock issue limited to an amount equal to subsidy payable to province. The proposed constitutional amendment would give your government power to withhold subsidy in the event of default by provinces. We have no objections to this. Our proposal sets out the extent to which we ask the assistance of your government and we feel that it can be carried out and that it limits your responsibility to an amount which will at all times be covered by the subsidy. In view of very limited nature of obligation which your government would assume under our proposal we trust you will assist us in meeting April first maturity and favorably consider our request.
William Aberhart.
On March 30, 1936, I sent the following telegram to Mr. Aberhart:
Ottawa, March 30, 1936. Hon. Wm. Aberhart,
Premier of Alberta,
Edmonton, Alta.
Your wire twenty-seventh has been considered by government. You state that you cannot agree to accept loan council arrangement. Nevertheless you ask us to assist in meeting your April first maturity and then you propose to go forward with program outlined in your previous wire involving change in maturities of and reduction of interest upon large portion of your outstanding debt. Not only would this involve unfair discrimination between holders of obligations maturing April first and holders of other securities but it.

Alberta Financial Situation
would cause all the injury to provincial credit which we have been doing our utmost to avoid. Regret very much that your decisions make it impossible for the dominion to assist you on April first. Nor can dominion government agree to ask parliament for authority to give dominion guarantee to your proposed partial refunding ^program under conditions outlined in your wires.
Chas. A. Dunning.
On the same day this telegram from Mr. Aberhart, addressed to myself, apparently crossed the one which I have just read:
Edmonton, Alta.,
March 30, 1936.
Hon. C. A. Dunning,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa, Ont.
Further to our wire twenty-seventh, if you assist us as requested to meet maturity we would agree to reimburse you to full amount from natural resources settlement as and when agreed upon. On this basis we would owe the dominion less than any western province. If you accept our proposal we are confident refunding plan can be carried out.
William Aberhart.
To that I replied on March 30, as follows:
Ottawa, March 30, 1936. Hon. Wm. Aberhart,
Premier of Alberta,
Edmonton, Alta.
Your wire thirtieth reached me in house after my wire giving government's decision had been dispatched. Your suggestion that natural resources settlement amounting to five million dollars and interest should be offset against new loan was made to me in January by your provincial treasurer. I pointed out to him that as in the case of Saskatchewan the natural resources award would have to be offset against debts already owing by provinces to dominion amounting in Alberta's case to twenty-four million seven hundred and forty-nine thousand dollars.
Chas. A. Dunning.
That, Mr. Speaker, completes the correspondence and tells the story much better than I could by any statement.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday on the orders of the day the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) asked for certain information with regard to a supplementary trade agreement recently concluded with France, and I promised to make a statement to-day. It is very brief. I might perhaps in fairness say, first, that the original negotiations were initiated by the former administration and concluded by the present one.
An exchange of notes between Canada and France was effected at Paris on March 20, 1936, whereby each country accorded to the other some concessions additional to those provided for under the trade agreement of May 12, 1933, and the additional protocol of February 26, 1935. The new arrangement came into force yesterday, March 31, 1936. The Canadian government agreed to make, by order in council, the following adjustments in favour of France.
Item 156(a)

Rum-intermediate tariff less a discount of 30 per cent.
Item ex 197 and ex 198-Cigarette paper, gummed or not, in rolls-intermediate tariff on item No. 197 less a discount of 30 per cent.
Item ex 199-Cigarette paper, gummed or not. in tubes, booklets or packets-intermediate tariff less 30 per cent.
In return the French government gives to Canada the minimum tariff of France on a number of commodities, including selenium, knitting machine needles, outboard motors and hairpins. I might say that the department has received numerous requests from Canadian exporters of these products who stated they could do business with France if they were given the benefit of the minimum tariff of that country.
In addition, France has agreed to continue quotas on porcelain insulators, electric heating apparatus and vacuum cleaners, which were enumerated in schedule F of the additional protocol of February 26, 1935. In the exchange of notes France also undertakes to grant Canada sympathetic treatment with respect to quotas generally. I might add that the further details were published in the edition of March 2S of the Commercial Intelligence Journal, of which every hon. member received a copy.

subtopic: EQUALIZATION OP PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO 1930 WHEAT CROP

speechtext: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) moved the third reading of Bill No. 22, to provide for the payment of certain sums of money to primary producers of wheat with respect to wheat of the 1930 crop delivered to provincial pool organizations.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: EQUALIZATION OP PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO 1930 WHEAT CROP
speechtext:
I am glad to see that the first minister is in his place for the first time since this bill has been engaging the attention of the house, because the legislation involves matters to which I desire particularly to direct his attention.
The circumstances connected with the introduction and explanation of this legislation are so extraordinary that I regard it as of first importance, on the third reading of this measure, that I should summarize the situation, for not only does it affect to-day but it is a precedent which, if followed, will

open up an avenue to which I do not believe the first minister, having regard to his high purposes with respect to the maintenance of the institutions of parliament, would desire to become a party.
The situation may be summarized very briefly. In 1935, at a session of this parliament, a measure was enacted that authorized and empowered a corporation created by this parliament, namely the Canadian wheat board, to acquire from the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, on terms and conditions to be approved by the governor in council, all stocks of wheat that they might hold at the time the board took those stocks over. The wheat held amounted to many millions of bushels, not only some seventy-five odd millions but that wheat which that cooperative enterprise had accumulated during the years from 1931 to 1935. That may be held to be agreed upon, and is common knowledge from the records. The second point to which attention is to be directed is that there was prepared and passed on October 10 an order in council by which what purported to be an agreement between the selling enterprise and the purchasing board was approved subject to auditors' certificates being produced to indicate the correctness of the figures which were employed in the body of the documents.
It will be recalled that during the progress of the discussion a memorandum from the former Minister of Finance was produced indicating that he had received from the then Prime Minister a memorandum upon which action had been taken. I pointed out that my memory was that no such memorandum had been prepared by me, but the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), as reported at page 14)81 of Hansard, referred to this memorandum and asked what were its contents. I told him that I could not undertake to speak as to its contents for I did not recollect ever having signed or made such a memorandum. He thereupon reasserted that it was an important state document and that it was too bad it was not then available. Yesterday, in reply on the second reading, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) produced a memorandum. It has not been laid upon -the table of the house, as I thought it had.

I was in an embarrassed position in view of what the Minister of Finance said, and I ask any minister of the crown to put himself in the same position as I was placed in by that observation. It was stated by the Minister of Finance at that time that the order in council had been prepared on the instructions of the then Prime Minister, and the Minister of Finance said that those instructions, of course, were state documents. I tried to show him that such was not the case, and I said that Mr. Paul Bredt, of the cooperative enterprises, had come to my car at Montreal and, he having made certain statements, Mr. R. K. Finlayson-I did not give his name yesterday-at my request came to Ottawa, Mr. Bredt accompanying him. I find on the file the memorandum that was prepared by Mr. Finlayson for the Department of Justice. At page 1645 of Hansard the Minister of Agriculture is reported as having said this:
Some reference was made last evening to a *document which I did not know at that time
was available. I have before me a copy of that document, and I take it off the file because it is impossible to read it without taking it off, for a very important part of it is under the clip on the file. That important part is also written in in pen and ink, across the top of the memorandum. It reads like this:
Instructions received from P.M. through R.K.F. on 8th October.
That document was produced by the minister from the file, and there are other documents on the file as well, including the order in council; I do not see it here now.

subtopic: EQUALIZATION OP PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO 1930 WHEAT CROP
speechtext: The memorandum is the second last document.

subtopic: EQUALIZATION OP PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO 1930 WHEAT CROP
speechtext:
The document has in writing these words:
Instructions received from P.M. through R.K.F. on 8th Oct. F.P.V.
In Hansard it appears "F.P.E." "F.P.V." are the initials of Mr. Varcoe, of the Department of Justice. That is in his handwriting and not mine nor that of anyone connected with me; and in order that the matter may be succinctly and logically placed upon Hansard I shall read the memorandum, which is as follows:
The Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, agree to sell to the Canadian wheat board, all wheat owned by them and all their contracts for the purchase of wheat, and to transfer and deliver the same to the Canadian wheat board immediately upon the acceptance of this offer, and upon the terms hereinafter set out.
(a)	The Canadian wheat board accepts as of the 31st day of August, 1935, all liabilities of the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, in respect of the said wheat and the said contracts for advances made in connection with the acquisition and the holding thereof by the following banks:-
As stated by the minister yesterday, the names of the banks are not given.
(b)	The amount to be paid by the Canadian wheat board to the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, is the sum of-
No figure being given.
-being the balance due to the primary producers for wheat and expenses and other charges in connection with the holding and handling thereof.
That is the entire memorandum which Mr. Varcoe's signature says was received from Mr. Finlayson, secretary, as indicating the instructions of the Prime Minister. That is the story up to that point. There is, however, attached to the file what was not read yesterday, namely, the memorandum which was sent to Mr. Rhodes, Minister of Finance, by the deputy minister. It says:
Dear Sir:	8th October, 1935.
At the request of Mr. R. K. Finlayson I have had prepared and enclose herewith for

Wheat Board-Mr. Bennett

your signature a report to council in connection with the proposed acquisition by the Canadian wheat board of wheat and contracts to purchase wheat from the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited. I understand that the letters set out in this report are to be exchanged to-day.
I assume that the president of the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, has been duly authorized to agree to the terms set forth and that the wheat board has or will have duly authorized its chairman to accept the offer.	,
With reference to the cash payment to be made to the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, for the purpose of paying certain claims advanced by their members in respect of wheat delivered in 1930, I nave, of course, no knowledge of the legality of these
claims.
Yours truly,
Deputy Minister.
The Honourable E. N. Rhodes,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa.
That of course is the first knowledge I have of that letter, obtained this afternoon from the files sent me just now, in the presence of members of this chamber, by the Minister of Agriculture. There we have the order in council situation, I think, clearly explained by the documents that were produced from the custody of the Department of Finance, the Department of Justice and the privy council office. They clearly indicate how the order in council came into being or was formed, to use the language of the Minister of Agriculture. Another expression used was to the effect that it was built up. I think that abundantly appears from the evidence that has now been presented. I deeply regret that no opportunity was afforded even to see these documents before they were used in reply, when I had exhausted my right to speak, and the only opportunity I have to clear up this situation and to place it in some form of continuity is on the third reading of this measure.
Then, let us proceed to the next point, which is very simple. Mr. Rhodes dispatched the order in council by messenger and it was signed as indicated'-the draft of the report, I should say, not the order in council. May I take that back and say that he dispatched to two ministers the report thus prepared and it was signed, under the circumstances set out, by one of them, the other not being accessible; and when it came to Toronto to the then president of -the privy council, or the Prime Minister, whichever you desire to say, he added to it the words: that these amounts should be certified by the auditors. My information is that the query was as to what warrant there was for these figures, and there being no certificate with respect to them the request was made in writing placed upon the

document that there should be provision for there being a certificate by auditors. And in that regard it will be remembered that when the order in council was passed on October 10 it was subject to the certificates of auditors with respect to the matters in question.
The document, dated October 5, produced yesterday by the Minister of Agriculture, was a certificate by auditors addressed to the cooperative enterprise at Winnipeg. How it came into the possession of the Department of Justice, I do not know, but it did not come from the office of the Prime Minister so far as I have been able to ascertain. I suspect at least-and I think I may say that without making any inference-that it came from Mr. Bredt who was here in the east at that time. That ends the order in council.
Shortly after that, to continue the narrative, the new Minister of Finance sent out instructions, which have been set out at length in Hansard, to the auditors asking that certain information should be furnished by them with respect to the transactions between the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited and the wheat board and the producers of grain during the whole period that they had operated in connection with the stabilization operations. That information from the auditors was not received until late in January, 1936. It would next appear that the new government, the present administration, at the request of the new chairman of the wheat board, required that the wheat owned by the cooperative enterprise should be turned over to the wheat board. Bear in mind that the quantity of wheat was not only that which was represented by the 1930 crop but also the additions that had been accumulated during the period in which the cooperative enterprise had operated. It will be remembered that last year the evidence given before the committee was that this amounted to a very large quantity, I think nearly 200,000,000 bushels in all, which they had accumulated during the progress of the stabilization operations carried on in the years intervening between 1931 and 1935.
It would next appear that the action of the cooperative enterprise in turning over wheat was not as rapid as the government desired and that there were certain difficulties to be overcome in connection with determining what was to be paid to the organization by the purchasers, the wheat board. That is. abundantly clear. But here again I regret, to say-and that is the reason I do direct the matter to the attention of the Prime Minister, who after all is responsible for the

Wheat Board-Mr. Bennett
conduct of business in the house, as I found out to my sorrow at times-the fact is that these documents indicating that something other than the order in council had been created were not produced in this chamber on the initial statement with respect to the matter, nor do they appear in the terms of ohe resolution which we have considered, nor do we hear of them until later, when the preamble of the bill became known to us and it there appeared that the wheat had actually been turned over to the new board on the second day of December, 1935'. Close reading of that so-called assignment will indicate that it was hardly sufficient for the purpose of turning over the visible wheat; it undertook to deal only with the contracts. It was not until December 17 that a memorandum was produced indicating that the wheat had in fact been turned over to the new board.
Now, sir, I suggest that there is not an hon. member in this chamber who heard the explanation given on the resolution who did not believe, as I did, that the government were proceeding under the order in council of October 10, and that owing to delays in connection with securing information from the auditors, negotiations had taken place for the purpose of settling terms that under the order in council would be settled by auditors' certificates. What was my surprise, and the surprise, I think, of most hon. members who had not any previous information, to find that instead of the order in council of October 10 being the important document which was responsible for the turning over of the wheat, it was the action taken by the government upon which a telegram had been sent by the Minister of Trade and Commerce threatening the cooperative enterprise with two grave results that would follow if they did not act promptly. One was that the government would avail itself of the provisions of the order in council and sell the wheat and wheat contracts, the other that the government would close off the credit of the cooperative enterprise by cancelling the guarantees. That, I think, is a fair statement of the situation up to that moment.
In view of the production of the documents to which I have referred, and the statement made in the preamble of the bill that the wheat was actually'turned over on December 2, I regard the situation as being one of very great importance, because the preamble of the bill is contradictory, as I shall presently point out. We have first of all the statement made yesterday by the minister, as reported at page 1652 of Hansard, that the order in 12739-108J
council of October 10, 1935, had ceased to have any value whatever. In order that there may be no misapprehension I read his statement:
But whoever pays will be the agent of the government in paying the money to the primary producer. The money is ours; it does not belong to the pool but passes through their hands to the people to whom we think it should go, the primary producers.
Mr. Bennett: That puts the order in council out of business.
Mr. Gardiner: That has always been out of business.
That has always been out of business 1 Now, in the face of that I do not think it is necessary to make any further reference. But there is another reference of the hon. gentleman to the matter, at page 1653 of Hansard, in exactly the same sense. I was reading from the documents and I said:
I object to the following words, which are at variance with the facts as produced by the minister. It was not under authority of paragraph (f) of section 7 of the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935, that this was done, at all.
Mr. Gardiner: I have never said so.
Now, there one has, without going into other statements which have the same meaning, a fair and clear indication, I submit, that the government-wholly within their rights -took the view that they wanted possession of that wheat for the wheat board, which in my judgment was a proper thing, because parliament had said that it should be done, and as the terms and conditions under which it was to be done had not been dealt with as provided for by order in council owing to the difficulty of getting the necessary information by way of certificates, the government took the position: We will sit down and make a settlement with you. And they made a settlement, because yesterday the Minister of Agriculture said: This has been agreed upon by everybody and you need not have any doubt about any wording. I will not take time again to read the statement into the record. It was said: You need not worry about taking time in connection with this, there will be no trouble about releases because this has been agreed upon.

speechtext: No, that is not it. The right hon. gentleman is not quoting my words.

subtopic: EQUALIZATION OP PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO 1930 WHEAT CROP
speechtext:
I could read them; they are here, but the point is that the hon. gentleman said when he was in western Canada during the by-election: If we cannot do this we will sit down and get together. Those words were in the quotation from the Leader-Post, as I read it the other evening indicating
Wheat Board-Mr. Bennett

what he proposed to do, namely negotiate a settlement. He therefore said distinctly and positively in terms that the settlement had been made.
Without going into that further, although possibly it might be important to do so, I desire, I repeat again, to direct the attention of the Prime Minister specially to the terms of the preamble of this bill. I do not think the Prime Minister would desire that the house should give its support to a preamble which is not in accordance with the facts. I point out that the language which is employed in this preamble is not even consistent, and is not in accordance with the facts. Yesterday I appealed as well as I knew how to the house to remedy the bill in this respect, but unfortunately party differences become so acute that anything that may be said by me with respect to the matter is regarded by the other side from a purely party point of view, and I suppose e converso, anything said by the other side is regarded on this side as being purely political. But I have an interest m this matter purely as a member of the House of Commons, and when I suggest to the chamber, as I do, that this preamble contains contradictory phrases, wholly at variance with what has been said by the minister, I state I think something that is axiomatic; it is apparent to whoever reads. The minister said last evening that he desired that this preamble should remain in its present condition because it was an historic record of the whole transaction from 1930 to date. If it is a matter of history there are two factors that must combine to give it value; it must be an impartial statement, and it must be accurate. If the statement is not impartial it is not a proper statement of facts. If it is inaccurate obviously it should not be in the preamble.
The rule with respect to preambles of private bills is that they must be proved; with respect to public bills the rule is that there must be evidence in the bill itself as a basis for the preamble. In chapter 61 of the statutes of Saskatchewan to which I referred yesterday there was a preamble. That preamble was based upon the agreement reached at the wheat conference in London in 1933. But the draftsman in that case pursued the course that is always pursued when a public bill carries with it a preamble with respect to which there may be difference of opinion as to the facts; there was attached to it as a schedule the agreement. The wheat agreement of 1933 signed in London was attached to the schedule as the basis upon which the preamble -was founded. Now, this document goes from . 
this chamber without a single annex or schedule showing the basis for any statement made in the preamble. Not a word. subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOR NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Last
evening for ten minutes I discussed the second reading of this bill. I may say that the principle of it surprises me. What this bill proposes is that a post mortem be conducted by a sevenfold commission system. As I said last night, I do not wish to see this parliament abdicate its functions and leave it to any commission to deal with this problem. This particular bill, as the house knows, interferes with the scope of the trade and industry commission act now before the supreme court. That bill, in effecting the regulation of trade and commerce, would have done a great deal for unemployment and we should not have needed this present measure at all. In my opinion if this bill passes we might as well abolish the Department of Labour. The department is getting statistics; the municipalities are getting statistics; the provinces are gathering statistics; we have a bureau of statistics; like the unemployed, we are "statis-ticked" to death.
The commonest error in politics, Lord Salisbury said, is sticking to the carcasses of dead policies. That is what the government is doing, so far as this particular bill is concerned. In my opinion it does not set up any long term policy or provide any cure whatever.

What is needed is that those who want to work shall be provided with useful employment, and nothing in the bill presented by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) will be any cure for unemployment. Also the bill interferes with business. It is an interference by amateurs with the corporate direction of one's business by industry; in fact, as the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence) said the night before last-and he uttered words of wisdom-one of the main causes of unemployment is the haphazard way in which legislators are imposing burdens and artificial barriers and restrictions on business and the amateur interference with the heads of business. You are going to hand over to a commission of seven figureheads parliament's sovereign powers, and it will interfere in time with the liberty of the subject and of business as well. It will prevent any redress or reference to the law courts, because the commission can make rules and regulations binding on business, over the heads of the law courts and over the head of this parliament. It amounts to what Lord Hewart has called "the new despotism," and will prevent any further discussion in this parliament of this question.
I have been in this house for ten or twelve years, and in my opinion it is time to stop pussyfooting with this question. Parliament itself must face the issue. The other day the minister spoke very elaborately; he talked for two and a half hours, and no doubt he could have gone on for five or six hours reading statistics which are not at all relevant to the issue. It will bring small comfort to the unemployed to hand them a bound copy of Carlyle. The minister says Carlyle was a great social reformer. No doubt he was, but I quoted last night a great Englishman, and qualified that by saying that as a matter of fact he was an Irishman; I referred to Edmund Burke, who said that government was a practical thing, not something to please the fancy or imagination of ordinary politicians.
I may sum up the cures and palliatives of the minister to date as follows: first, the ambassador cure; next, the supreme court cure. We should now have contributory unemployment insurance for the working classes but for the fact that the Liberal party at the last session sat back and did nothing and then sent it to the supreme court of Canada. The present leader of the opposition in this parliament, who is a statesman if ever there was one, introduced a bill in this matter, for the first time since confederation, under the powers for the proper regulation of trade and commerce. Where is that bill to-day? They have had insurance in

Employment Commission-Mr. Church
England since 1909. They have had labour exchanges. They have them in the United States. And the government refers this legislation to the supreme court. One of the chief reasons why Great Britain has recovered is the fact that in that country they have unemployment insurance since 1909, and an efficient labour department. The duplication of commissions, the handout cure, bonuses, subventions and subsidies to some and not to others lack of equality of treatment, and last but not least the Thomas Carlyle cure-all these quack medicines and palliatives will produce no results. They will not mean another job for another man in this dominion. The farmers are not to be fooled on this April Fool's day; they will not stand for it any longer. The first of May is coming, spring is approaching, and bricklayers, carpenters and artisans are waiting for work; but the minister assures a deputation of municipalities that he is appointing a commission to get the facts. Well, the working classes in this country have all the facts right now; they do not have to rely on any neatly bound volume of Thomas Carlyle and other social reformers, including the professor who is now Minister of Labour, to tell them what ought to be done. They know only too well what ought to be done; what they want is work.
This bill is based on one principle and one principle only, laissez-faire, do nothingism- letting things be referred to useless commissions consisting of figureheads, the policy of muddling through. This policy, perilous and costly as it was during the war, is still more dangerous in times of peace, especially in connection with this particular department. The minister no doubt thinks that his bill, No. 14, is a solution of the unemployment problem. I do not think it is, nor do I regard any of his quack medicines or pills as a cure for the unemployment situation. He offered us nothing in his discourse the other day of two and a half hours. All we have is a policy of standing still, free trade, the teachings of the Manchester school; but I repeat that none of these things will end unemployment. The unemployed are becoming alarmed over parliament's failure to accomplish anything to relieve the situation. We have been here for two months and we do nothing; we do nothing but sit here and talk while jobs are wanted.
I am strongly opposed to this commission idea. We might as well go back home, for all the powers of parliament are being handed over to various commissions. Commissions are superseding parliament, they are taking over the prerogatives of the House of Commons; the passing of rules and regulations, magna charta, everything is being handed over
to these commissions. We have in this country what I would call commission government and I would suggest that all the commissions that have been appointed should be mobilized outside these parliament buildings and placed under the command of the hon member for Rimouski (Sir Eugene Fiset), who seems to be an expert in giving signs and high signs in this house. These commissions should be lined up with their staffs, their executives, their sisters, their cousins and their aunts, all of whom have been loaded on the commissions, with these who are to advise and recommend to the minister under Bill 14, and they would constitute a regular standing army in themselves. It is said that Canada has no standing army. I say that in these commissions, with their staffs and various employees, and the others referred to, we have a standing army the line up of wrhich would extend two deep from here to Lansdowne park. We should mobilize them in front of the parliament buildings and then demobilize them, and the sooner we do that the better for the working classes, and let parliament function.
Last night I quoted from the first verse, twelfth chapter of Ecclesiastes. "Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth"; to-day I might add that other famous eighth verse, "Vanity of vanities, saith the preacher; all is vanity." The vanity of commission rule. What are we doing in this house? We are simply sitting here and unloading our functions and powers on a political commission. The unemployed are asking for jobs and bread and we are giving them a stone in the shape of a commission, one of the most useless commissions ever appointed. We hear nothing but a lot of platitudes and high sounding phrases from English authors. We do not need any commission to study this question; what we need is a committee of this house. We appointed a committee to deal with deficits in railways and shipping, one of the most important problems with which the House of Commons has to deal, and that committee functions all right. A committee of the house should study and control unemployment. Here, as I say, we are turning over our powers to this commission.
The solution of this problem calls for widespread national sacrifice and not parliamentary repartee. This problem cannot be solved by majorities in parliament, it cannot be solved by any carnival of statistics. You can gather up all the statistics you like and we shall be no closer to a real solution of the problem. We must have a remedy as far-reaching as conscription was in the war. I believe in Christian socialism and of this kind-the socialism of
1702	COMMONS
Employment Commission-Mr. Church
Charles Kingsley and of the Oxford and evangelical movements of a hundred years ago. Those principles of socialism if applied in Canada might not create a new Jerusalem, but at any rate if run with horse sense they would rid this country of middlemen, parasites and shark loan companies and do something that would really help the unemployed. Sacrifice is the only cure for all Canada's ills-sacrifice and the right application of the doctrine of protection for all of the people all of the time and not for some of the people some of the time.
In his long discourse Monday the Minister of Labour could not retain his audience; the galleries for the most part, walked out, and no wonder. And a large part of the chorus of 245 members also begged leave to retire while the hon. gentleman was placing on Hansard tables that were not relevant to the question. A brilliant newspaper man who had edited a prominent journal in this country for forty years once told me that it was not worth five cents of news publicity having a representative here because the people took no stock in what parliament did. As far as this particular bill is concerned, I suggest that what we need is something that would prevent contentious amateur interference with industry and agriculture, interference that has placed so many artificial barriers and burdens upon business so that it cannot function. If the government and the Minister of Labour had to be elected by plebiscite, how many members of the present cabinet would be returned? I say, they have no mandate from the people. The government is here to-day simply because in October last the Canadian people, like the people in every country, were opposed to any government. The deep resentment against all governments the world over elected this government. I say that hon. gentlemen opposite should honour the task for which they have been elected. I agree with what the hon. member for Parkdale said the other night with regard to interference with business. The great mass of the intelligent electorate are not concerned with this game of ins and outs; they are not concerned with party politics, in connection with this problem at any rate. In my opinion the electors of Canada will assert the supremacy of the national over the party interest and shall insist upon their elected representatives discharging their plain duty to the country. They should insist on the private member functioning and should require him to do his duty to his constituents in order to help to rebuild the social and economic structure. The country is sick of politics and we want a

new set of rules for the game. The people do not want the dole, which is only a temporary remedy; they want work, for that is the only lasting form of unemployment relief.
The minister read extensively from Thomas Carlyle, but that is not the type of reading that appeared on the billboards in Toronto and in other counties in October lasrt- "Action, not promises. End unemployment. Vote Liberal. Beat Bennett and Bad Times." On a billboard on Queen Street, Toronto, painted in black and yellow, the colours of the well known racing stable; it said, "End unemployment; vote Snelgrove." Well, the unemployed are still carrying the black flag, and this proposal is nothing but the yellowest kind of yellow as a palliative for the cure of unemployment. Platforms, the late Hon. J. Israel Tarte once said, were made to get in on, not to stand on. But the unemployed will not much longer put up with this kind of thing.
The minister speaks of a publicity campaign. We had an illustration of that the other day in the case of a large department store that in my opinion, is using its employees in any but a proper way, and I know something about it because I go in there quite often. This particular company just snaps its fingers at this parliament and anything it can do. In my opinion the Minister of Labour should look into these complaints about sweat shops and child labour and the way these people are going on with the legislation referred to the supreme court. The liberty of the press, the fourth estate, has been assailed. We should open the tower upstairs and bring some of these gentlemen to the bar of the house as was done in the days of Cinq Mars, and find out who is running this country, and whether these large department stores are to be permitted to intimidate the press and parliament in this way.
This bill forgets all about the suburban workers; also those of our community whom Disraeli called the suffering millions are entirely forgotten. I asked this house twelve years ago, in 1924, to adopt this policy of appointing an economic commission to investigate unemployment. At that time Senator Couzens, the former mayor of Detroit and governor of Michigan, conducted a most exhaustive inquiry into unemployment and this bill is very largely based on the findings off that commission. Many of the recommendations which have been adopted in this bill have been proved to be wrong in many respects, especially the commission and the index

Employment Commission-Mr. Church
principle. I have not three and a half hours at my disposal or I would take it up in detail and show the errors made in handling this problem. In the nature of things there can be no statistics on unemployment without a census. If a census were taken so that we have the number of unemployed at a given time the Department of Labour could apply their index. This bill furnishes no definition of what is meant by an unemployed person. The labour department under its system of enumerating industries has shown a faulty calculation. In my opinion the only way to approach the problem of unemployment is to have a complete census taken at some definite date. The tables quoted by the minister are of little or no value; they are incomplete and merely preliminary. Elaborate forms are sent out to be filled in, but the history of unemployment in the United States shows that such a procedure is often wrong.
This bill does not define unemployment. The term "unemployed" I understand to mean a person who, usually in work, is seeking a job. It does not include people who are too old to hold a job or who are unemployable for other reasons, people who rightly belong to the outdoor relief class, for which industry is not immediately responsible. The figures relating to these people form a sociological table, not one for the statistics of the department. I can see no object in appointing this form of commission.
A word or two about the municipalities, which have had to bear the brunt throughout these years. Direct aid should be given to the large municipalities, not to the provinces only. The federal government should take over the entire cost of the administration of relief of unemployment, and the larger municipalities should be given equality of treatment with some of the provinces that have been in difficulty during the last five or six years, because the problem is a federal one.
I was disappointed in the minister's speech the other day. I failed to find any reference to many important features of the situation. We have a war in Canada to-day, a war between millions of our fellow men and poverty and starvation, a war between youth and poverty. The enemy is just as dangerous as a foreign foe in war time. Against a foreign foe we unite; against our internal foe we are disunited and do nothing to check or repel it. When the invader is at our gates the country mobilizes its entire resources, its man power, its transportation system, its capital, but in time of depression and unemployment driving people to the wall the
industrial workers are left without any protection at all; they bear the brunt and we do nothing but sit around and appoint commissions. Nothing is said in this bill as to the relation between the industrial worker and agriculture.
I would like to say a word or two in relation to industrial employment, because I want to contrast with the precepts of Christianity the way the industrial workers are used. Contrast our professions with the ruthless competition, the cruelty and vice of present day business and industry. Here personality counts as nothing, the dollar is all supreme. Modern life is machine life, soulless, a life of standardization, high speed production, a highly efficient organization for the making of profit. Everything is done in the mass, and life is made uniform, monotonous and artificial. Dividends are the chief objective; to get dividends human beings are sacrificed. Wages are shockingly low, often below the level of mere subsistence, so that people are forced into immoral and criminal ways of life to eke out a precarious livelihood. The maximum in hours of work is exacted in return for the minimum in wages. Senior employees, whose lifeblood has been drawn from them by long years of faithful service, are in many cases cast out without retiring allowance to make room for younger and cheaper people. It matters not what suffering is entailed for human beings so long as the stockholders are paid their dividends. This amazing selfishness and shortsightedness of the modern industrial system is creating a progressively lower standard of living and a vicious struggle for existence philosophy on the part of the people, increasingly serious social problems which must find their tragic solution either in war or in revolution. In the face of modern methods of competitive living the royal law of love, bear ye one another's burdens and so fulfil the law of Christ, is a hollow mockery in Canada, presumably a Christian country. This is the contradiction of modern life: a truly wonderful appreciation of the value of the single soul in some quarters, but an absolute denial of any such value in others
With all this unemployment around us we sit here and make provision for individual groups. We support vast numbers of public institutions; we provide protection for the under-privileged and weak; we place medical and scientific knowledge in the hands of people who can use it for the preservation of life, and particularly did we do so in the
1704	COMMONS
Employment Commission-Mr. Church
case of the Dionne children. We do all this, but we do nothing to protect our industrial workers.
In conclusion may I say a word about the government's unemployment policy as it affects agriculture. I would like to see a maximum production of farm products, and would also like to see a close cooperation between agricultural and industrial producers; for the great and extensive needs of agriculture must be supplied. Prosperous industry depends upon a prosperous agriculture, and the Conservative party has always been associated with the development of agriculture. It is one industry which has not rallied to communist propaganda. I should like to see agriculture in Canada developed by a comprehensive plan, and one which would be adapted to Canada's situation. That could be done by the collaboration of the provincial representatives of agricultural departments with people concerned with industry, and in that way the whole rural population of Ontario would be lifted to a higher collective life. It could be done, not by ruining anybody but by merging single interests into one united national endeavour to develop agriculture in all its forms. In that way we would lift our country to a higher economic and social plane. Every individual should be engaged in this work.
May I observe, further, that the government will have to open up their ranks to new men and their minds to new ideas. There should be a modification of the present parliamentary system; otherwise a socialist government would be possible. The government of the day must be a constructive force for the building of a healthy society, based on economic and spiritual freedom, or give place to those who have a constructive program as an alternative to socialism. The progressive Conservatives are the hope of the country. Such a policy may be unpopular in parliament, but if this fight is carried outside the ring the rules of the party will be broken. The government's policy of setting up commissions is not popular. There can be no question about the personal integrity of government leaders, but their political wisdom is questioned. The opening processional hymn of praise of hon. members who have spoken about the minister disappoints even those who might agree with their policies, and I was sorry to see my friend the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) indulge in flattery. The man on the street knows that the government party machine is fighting for its own life and not for the country or the majority of the people. Their grasp of the post-war problems is feeble.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the motion is adopted I should like to say a few words regarding unemployment as it exists in the province of Prince Edward Island. First, however, may I congratulate the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) upon the masterly manner in which he has presented to the house the measure now before us.
Before proceeding to further observations may I at least to some extent reply to the remarks of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) and, as the time before adjournment is short, I shall be brief. The hon. member admits that unemployment is the most important problem remaining to be solved, and in the next breath he states that the appointment of an employment commission illustrates the decay of parliament. As I see it, sir, hon. gentlemen opposite have watched the decay of parliament in the last five years and they cannot now appreciate its resurrection. The hon. member for Broadview referring to the National Employment Commission states that it is all right to put your name down on a list, but that it would be easy for the minister to wipe it off with a sponge. Earlier in his speech he condemned the appointment of such a commission, and stated in effect that the department should look after the unemployed. May I point out to him that one of the objects in the appointment of a commission is the elimination of political interference. The hon. member stated further that he was not in agreement with the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey), and that he believed the youth of Canada would not find jobs through the operations of a commission. He stated still further that by itself the government could not pull the country out of the mire. May I say to him that one reason the commission is being appointed is that the government realizes the importance of the problem, and believes that the matter cannot be handled by any governmental department.
I was amazed to hear the hon. member for Broadview criticize the minister for referring to Thomas Carlyle, the great writer, who died many years ago. Well, Carlyle died in 1881, but the hon. member immediately proceeded to call to his support, as recorded in Hansard, an Englishman named Edmund Burke. As

Employment Commission-Mr. Grant
a matter of fact Edmund Burke was an Irishman, like the hon. member, and died in 1797, about ninety years before Carlyle's death.
May I preface my further remarks by an illustration:	Let us suppose that England
should be forced into a European war and that Canada should decide to enter the war at the side of the mother country. Could not this country afford to send three hundred thousand young men overseas for four or five years and pay them $1.10 a day to shoot down our enemies? I do not say that we should send them or that we would send them, but I do say that this country sent them before and paid them $1.10 a day, and in addition fed them and clothed them and housed them. To that end the government committed this country to millions and millions of dollars of debt for generations to come. Then why cannot this government help the poor farmers of Prince Edward Island and other provinces, who are so hard pressed for assistance, by paying that same wage to the young men who are now idle, in order that they may work for farmers who need their help? The farmers would clothe and feed them, but they have not the money to pay them wages. The only difference would be that the government would be relieved in this case of feeding and clothing and housing the men, and the country would not be committed to many millions of dollars of present'and future expenditure. That is one way, Mr. Speaker, that I see in which this government could help put unemployed young men to wrnrk, especially in the province of Prince Edward Island. I have in my constituency perhaps seventeen jobs on boats, and I had four hundred applicants for those seventeen jobs.

Working on tugs and
dredges, and of course everybody who is a Liberal and unemployed is now looking to me for a job. How do you expect me, Mr. Speaker, to divide four hundred into seventeen without getting anything but a fraction? We will have plenty of friction, I can assure you of that.
I realize that different localities require different remedies, and as far as the province of Prince Edward Island is concerned, it is not practicable to put many men to work on the railways, especially if they are going to be operated in the same manner in which they were run during the last five years. In that case we might put a few men to work greasing the track to keep the rails from rusting. That will give you an idea of the sort of railway service we have had in Prince Edward Island during the last five years.
So far as business men and tradesmen are concerned, they are prosperous in our province when the farmers and fishermen are prosperous, and prosperity will come to the former when you put the farmers and the fishermen on their feet.
The province of Prince Edward Island has been neglected for the last five years. It has been allowed to fade off the map. I remember well the famous radio speeches delivered in January, 1935, by the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). Those speeches were printed in book form and distributed among the electors of this country. I received five of them. There was a map of Canada on the front page of the book, and would you believe it, Mr. Speaker, Prince Edward Island was left off that map entirely.

speechtext: Shame.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOR NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, Prince
Edward Island, the most important province in Canada, the cradle of confederation, was left off the map that appeared on the front page of that book of radio speeches, and yet our province, I repeat, was the cradle of confederation and the birthplace of the great Sir Louis Davies and of the Macphails and Schurmans and of many others of the world's most famous literary men and women; and only recently we had the honour of returning as one of our representatives the Minister of Finance, and we have every confidence that he will stand up for the rights of Prince Edward Island.
But while Prince Edward Island was left off the map in those books of reform speeches, it has been put on the map in some other ways in recent months, and right here I wish to pay a tribute to the memorj' of the late Hon. Walter M. Lea who put Prince Edward Island back on the map last summer one hundred per cent, so that to-day our local legislature is in session with thirty members on one side of the house and none on the other. Prince Edward Island was again put on the map on the fourteenth of October last, and again one hundred per cent, to cooperate with the federal government in ridding Prince Edward Island and the rest of Canada of unemployment.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, public works afford a measure of relief, but that relief is only temporary, and if some arrangement such as I have suggested could be made whereby the government would assist our farmers in securing young men to help work on the farms, the government paying them for a limited length of time. Such an arrangement would be far better than any unnecessary public works. Necessary public works, of course, must go on; we must have them,

i706
Employment Commission-Mr. Grant
and we insist on having our share of them in Prince Edward Island, but there are in our province thousands of farmers who need help and cannot get it because they have not the money to pay out in wages. Again I would impress upon the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) the fact that there are thousands of young men idle to-day in Prince Edward Island; why not pay them $1.10 a day to go to work for the farmers who need their help, and who will willingly supply them with good food, and shelter.
I am one hundred per cent for this bill, Mr. Speaker, . because no government can handle such an important problem as unemployment as it exists in Canada to-day in a routine manner. You may call this a commission or what you will, but something of the kind is necessary, and the men who are to serve on the commission must give this unemployment problem their whole time and concentrated energy because it is a very responsible work that they are called upon to do. When hon. members say we do not need a commission for this purpose, I am afraid they are not sincere. The only thing I see wrong with this bill is that it comes five years too late. Not four years but five years of wasted effort.
In conclusion, sir, I would urge the Minister of Labour to hasten a solution of this unemployment problem, and to see to it that so far as it is -humanly possible, full and equal justice be done to every part of Canada.

On the orders of the day:

Before the orders of the day are called, Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct two or three questions to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). The questions are based on a report in the western press of March 26 and 30, covering questions asked at the session of the provincial legislature as to oats futures and cash oats purchased by the provincial government during the winter of 1934-35.
