The house resumed from Wednesday, April 1, consideration of the motion of Hon. Mr. Rogers for the second reading of Bill No. 14, respecting the establishment of a national employment commission.

subsubtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOR NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
In rising to say a few words on the second reading of this bill I wish first to extend my congratulations to the minister upon the very comprehensive information he gave us in his speech of Monday last, and. also upon the very reasonable and reasoned way in which he dealt with this question. It is essential if we are to find a solution for a problem of this kind, one which is of such
1710	COMMONS
Employment Commission-Mr. Maclnnis
great importance in this country to-day, that we approach it in a reasonable and dispassionate manner. I quite understand that it is not easy for everyone to do that, especially those who are suffering from the effects of unemployment, but I think we who are here can do it in that way if we try. I hope the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) will not consider this a weakening of my moral fibre, because I am not going to congratulate the minister on this measure. I can congratulate him neither on the bill nor on the social philosophy which he expounded to the house when speaking to the bill.
I quite understand that on the second reading of a bill we can deal only with its general principle. The principle of the bill is the appointment of a national commission on employment. The minister stated that the long continued unemployment which we have had for the last five or six years is a challenge to our political intelligence. I quite agree with him in that, but I do not see that the bill in its present form can or will do much to provide a solution of the problem. The main function of the national employment commission will be the gathering of statistics. Other functions will be to recommend certain things to the minister and to promote cooperation between the various agencies that deal with relief. So far as that goes I am quite in agreement with it; I believe it is a necessary beginning. But I do not believe that this bill will in any way satisfy the people of Canada who voted for this government in order that the problem of unemployment should be solved. The speech from the throne stated that unemployment was Canada's most urgent national problem. This bill is a very inadequate measure to deal with that most urgent national problem.
As I have said, the main function of the national employment commission to be created by this bill will be the gathering of information in regard to unemployment. If unemployment is Canada's most urgent national problem I believe we should have delegated to this or to some other commission the function of trying to ascertain the cause of unemployment. Unemployment in itself is not a cause; it is an effect; and it does not make very much difference how many statistics we gather in regard to it, they are not going to get us very far in determining the cause. My opinion is that we can no more find the cause of unemployment by collecting statistics as to numbers, sex, age, occupation, vocation and so on of those unemployed than we can determine

the cause of cyclones by examining the wreckage they leave in their wake. The unemployed are the wreckage left as a result of certain economic conditions, and to examine the victims and tabulate them is not to find the solution for unemployment.
We were told that when the new government took office we would have a new policy for this great national problem. It seems to me that the policy of the present government differs very little from the policy of the last government. Possibly we are going to have more statistics, but whether or not these statistics will give a greater measure of relief for those who are unemployed, and give them more of the advantages of society than they now have, I am not prepared to say. I do not know whether anyone else is prepared to make a statement on that point. There is one danger however that I should like to point out in connection with the creation of the commission, and that is the potential danger of its coming between the people and the government. I do not know whether that condition will arise, but I should like to know to what extent the commission will have that effect. I am disturbed on the point, because I 'believe it has been greatly to the advantage of the unemployed during the last five years to be in a position where they could confront various governments with their problems. But if now they are to be compelled to go to the commission, a commission over whom they have no control, I am afraid conditions will become serious.
I note that when the mayors' conference met certain members of the cabinet a few days ago the Minister of Labour made this statement: as reported in the Vancouver Province of March 26: "If the commission had been in existence the conference of mayors would have been referred to it." Is that the situation we are to have when we approach the government on matters affecting the unemployed? Will the government refer us to the commission? If so, I do not believe that that will be satisfactory. I say we should still be in a position where we can approach those who are responsible for the administration of the affairs of the dominion.
When we were debating the resolution, before the bill was introduced, I pointed out that the measure contains no policy to deal with unemployment. The commission is supposed only, or at least to a great extent, to gather statistics. The only indication we have had of the government's policy has been in the speech of the Minister of Labour in moving the second reading of the bill.
One peculiar circumstance is that while the bill is submitted by a government which

Employment Commission-Mr. Maclnnis
believes in private ownership and private operation of industry, in the twenty-four lines of preamble the word "cooperate" or one of its derivatives appears five times. I have no objection to cooperation; as a matter of fact I am in favour of it. I favour a society based on cooperation, but the minister favours one based on competition. How does he expect to get cooperation in a society which must live, if it is going to live at all, by different sections of it competing with and taking advantage of each other? It seems to me that this constitutes a contradiction. As matters stand now, in order that some of us may work we must find ways and means of putting others out of work. That was -brought forcibly to my attention in an article written by Chapin Hoskins, managing editor of Forbes magazine, appearing in the November issue of Canadian Business. Dealing with the improvement in office equipment since the depression he states:
Two things, you see, have been happening during the depression. One is that businesses everywhere have been under the absolute necessity, since 1930, of cutting, cutting, cutting their costs, and particularly their overhead costs.
That is true not only of one business but of all kinds of business; in order to exist in a competitive world they must cut, cut, cut costs; and in order to cut costs they must displace labour with machinery. And let us remember that machinery does not consume or buy goods.

subsubtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOR NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: But the people who make the machines do.

subsubtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOR NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Quite so; the people who make the machines do. But if machines would not displace labour and reduce costs they would not be made. While I am on this point I should like to say that although I am not a prophet I can tell those in industry to-day how long they will remain employed. Under the present system they will remain employed until a machine is made wnich will do the work cheaper than they are doing it. When it is made they will find themselves out on the street, looking in at the machine. The development of machinery is continuing.
I should like to quote briefly from the minister's speech, because it is only by reading his speech that we can have any understanding of its underlying philosophy. The minister is reported at page 1591 as follows:
I have suggested that a sufficiency of food and shelter, clothing and medical attention must be provided for those in need. That is not in dispute.
I agree that that is not in dispute, but the measure in which it is given is in dispute. We have not yet decided what is a sufficiency. The minister continues:
In making this provision, however, there is equally an obligation upon governments to see that the arrangements for relief do not encourage the acceptance of voluntary idleness by relief recipients, or permit employers of labour to transfer to the state their obligation to pay a living wage and to conduct their operations with a due sense of social responsibility. I mention that here because some cases have been brought to my attention of employees of labour who have taken advantage of the existing situation and have paid wages upon so low a scale that those receiving those wages were receiving less than they would obtain if they were on relief.
That is not a new situation. It has been before this country for almost two years now, I think. The price spreads investigation, both the committee and the commission, brought out very definite and voluminous evidence on that very situation, nevertheless it would seem that as yet nothing has been done about it.
Someone was good enough to send me a few days ago a copy of the Evening Times-Globe, of Saint John, New Brunswick. I find in its issue of February 19, 1936, statements made by Chief Inspector McLeese, the County Treasurer, and another official named George H. Simpson. The news comment on the situation in Saint John is as follows:
A pitiful picture of unemployment conditions in certain Saint John industrial plants, a picture of sweat shop wages, of veteran employees being replaced by youths at apprentices' pay, and of full time workers earning so little that they are forced to seek direct relief, was given by Chief Inspector McLeese.
The statement goes on:
"Children have died this winter for no other reason in the world than that they were undernourished," the inspector declared. At the same time W. A. Ross, county treasurer and relief director, told of stores that had slashed wages of younger employees to such an extent that they were no longer able to help their parents by paying board. "Unemployment conditions in Saint John," declared Warden Simpson, "are rotten to the core."
I am not suggesting, Mr. Speaker, that the conditions referred to in the city of Saint John are any worse than those in any other city, but the fact remains that it was brought to the attention of this parliament a year and a half ago that these conditions existed in every part of Canada, and yet nothing has been done about it.
What does the minister suggest that we should do to-day? He says-I am quoting from the same page of Hansard:
It does seem to me that if on investigation we find an employer of labour who is taking
1712	COMMONS
Employment Commission-Mr. Maclnnis
advantage of this situation, we as a government are entitled to use the weapon of publicity to the fullest possible extent in order to brand that policy as high treason to the state in a time of great emergency.
Well, Mr. Speaker, this is the first time I ever heard that publicity was the penalty for high treason. I do not know very much law, but my impression is that sedition is a less grave offence than high treason, and yet we have our statute books full of penalties for those who are guilty of sedition. The minister suggests publicity for those who are guilty of the offence of high treason, but we provide section 98 for the unemployed. And then somebody will tell me that we have not class government in this country!
I should like to quote further from this Saint John paper to show how we deal with the unemployed in this country. It says:
"People," said Inspector McLeese, "don't realize what conditions are."
He told of the constant inspections the police were making-dropping in unexpectedly on families receiving relief. Picturing the extreme poverty existing in many cases, he described how a woman got a chance to go to work, but the prospective employer required that she be vaccinated. She spent three days trying to make arrangements to be vaccinated before, in despair, she appealed to the police, who were able to get her looked after.
Another man, with a bad tooth, his jaw all swollen on one side, and suffering extremely, appealed for help. He told the inspector he had been to the hospital, where he was informed that if he called again Wednesday, clinic day, he would be given an examination, and his tooth would be pulled the following Wednesday.
If he lived that long. And yet we get a bill such as the one now before us to deal with a situation like that! If you accept the principles of capitalism, is there really anything particularly wrong in an employer taking advantage of the situation that exists because of unemployment? Let us consider it in this way, the way it really is:	In order
to live, each one of us must have something to sell. The only thing which the worker has to sell is his labour power. All of us, when we buy the things we want, buy according to the way the goods are sold on the market. We buy bacon by the pound, cotton by the yard, wheat by the bushel, electric energy by the horsepower, and when we buy human energy, which is the only thing the worker has to sell, we buy it by the hour, the day or the month, as the case may be. In buying these things, how many of us ask how the product that we are buying was made. Did the labour that went into that product receive its just reward, its just remuneration? Of course we do not ask those
rMr. Maclnnis.]
questions. If the minister, for instance, were going to buy a house, and he saw one that suited him, and found that the price was very low because the man who owned it had to sell at a sacrifice price in order to save something out of it', would the minister or anyone else refuse to buy it on that account? Of course not. Do we not crowd the stores on bargain days in order to take advantage of someone's necessity to sell? And the question I would put, Mr. Speaker, is this: Where is the moral issue in this matter, provided again that you accept the principles of capitalism? There is none whatsoever.
Somewhere in his speech the minister made the statement that we needed statistics in order to get a more scientific approach to the question of unemployment. I may not agree with the minister but I do contend that the condition of unemployment itself affects people because it is a condition that comes between the people and their means of subsistence, and in my view you can approach the question scientifically only when you study unemployment in its relation to the means of production. But the commission is not asked to do that. What is that relation now? How do we get access to the means of production? A few own, but the great mass of the people, all of those who are unemployed, can get access to the means of production only by approaching someone who has the tools and the means by which they can work. Fortunately or unfortunately, employers of labour will employ labour only when they can profitably use it, and that is only when they can employ it at a profit to themselves.
We should also like to know-we should know-what this social relationship is going to be like as the years go on and technological improvements and further concentration of ownership continues. The minister very adroitly sidestepped this matter of technological development. The member for Peace River (Mr. Pelletier) asked the minister whether he believed that private industy would be able to absorb all the unemployed who are employable. The minister replied by making a long quotation from Thomas Carlyle. The member for Peace River then said: "Modern machinery makes it that much worse to-day." and the minister replied with another quotation from Carlyle. Then the member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) asked this question:	"Do the
statistics referred to give any indication as to what are termed respectively cyclical and technological unemployment? The minister's answer was, "I am not sure that we

Employment Commission-Mr. Maclnnis
can obtain that type of information, but I shall be glad to look into the possibility." In my opinion that is the crux of the question in dealing with unemployment. Unless we know to what extent people are to become unemployed or to get employment, unless we are to know to what extent the technological development of industry is going to affect employment in the days and the years to come, we can get no real idea of the implications of the factor of unemployment itself.
When some of us press for a better deal for the unemployed we are sometimes met with the statement that we are asking the government to do too much. The minister said that no government unaided could deal with this matter. Yet the question could be very well asked, what should be the function of government? Before answering that question we should possibly first ask, what is government? Should it not be an instrument of the people to do for the people collectively what they are unable to do for themselves? The function of governments in the past, and apparently their function at the present time, may be described as the maintenance of sufficient force to prevent the great masses of people who are deprived of access to the means of production from committing overt acts. In my opinion that is not the proper function of government. In a country like this, possessing enormous natural resources, great and efficient machinery of production, willing workers, and the technical skill and management necessary to run industry, the function of a government should be to bring these things together in order to create the essentials of a full life- not merely the means of subsistence, food, clothing and shelter, but everything that properly enters into the lives of the people. The minister made the statement:
I have suggested that a sufficiency of food and shelter, clothing and medical attention must be provided for those in need.
As I said before, we have not decided what 'sufficiency" means. We have come to a conclusion as to what is a balanced ration for horses, hogs, cattle and poultry, but we have not come to a conclusion as to what is a balanced diet for children. We have not yet come to a conclusion as to how much food and what kind is required so that they will not lose their teeth before they get out of their teens. The minister goes on:
The greatest resource of any country consists of its workers with hand and brain.
That is a very capitalistic statement-"the greatest resource of any country is its

workers." To my mind the workers are part of the country.
The greatest resource of any country consists of its workers with hand and brain. This in the ultimate analysis is the true wealth of nations. Upon its labouring population the state depends for its productivity and its real income in terms of goods and services.
And again:
It is to the interest of the state, quite apart from the question of obligation, to preserve the health and vigour of its people and as far as possible to prevent the impairment of the technical skill and efficiency of its workers.
To my mind that seems almost callous. It speaks of the workers in the same way as we would speak of our cattle and our machinery. It is necessary to preserve them, it is necessary to build shelters to keep them from the elements in order that when we need them we shall have them unimpaired. That, as I say, is not my idea of the function of government.
I agree with the minister, and I am glad we have it from him, that labour produces all wealth. But I would go a step further and say that when an owning class or a ruling class loses control of its labour it has lost everything it ever had, no matter how great its wealth, because without that control of the working class, no matter how great the employers' possessions, the owning class would have to go out and moil and toil in order to produce its own food. We have heard the minister, in this callous way, say that the duty of the government is to give the workers a sufficiency so that when we need them tomorrow in any capacity they will be available.
As far as the bill relates to the gathering of statistics, I have no objection to the measure. But it is certainly inadequate; it certainly falls short of what the people of this country expected at this time. In my opinion there is nothing sadder than to see a young and otherwise brilliant mind clinging to the shibboleths and traditions of the past, when these once useful traditions have lost their validity.
Sometimes I too, like the Minister of Labour, "for moral discipline and mental exercise," turn to the pages of Carlyle. Of all his striking passages the one which I am about to quote seems to me to explain most clearly the cause of the conditions facing society today. This is taken from the first volume of the French Revolution:
The widow is gathering nettles for her
children's dinner; a perfumed seigneur, delicately lounging in the Oeil de Boeuf, has an alchemy whereby he will extract from her the third nettle and name it rent and law. Such an arrangement must end.
1714	COMMONS
Employment Commission-Mr. McGeer
I was hoping that we could have the assistance of the Minister of Labour; I was hoping that he would be a material improvement over the late Minister of Labour, and as a matter of fact I am willing to go so far as to say he is. But I was hoping that he could go much further. My hon. friend from Broadview, I think it was, twitted him for being a professor. I regret that my acquaintance with professors has been rather meagre; I wish it had been greater; but from the little acquaintance I have had with them, I think we could do with more professors and fewer lawyers in parliament, and I hope that some time that situation will come about.
What was the arrangement which Carlyle said must come to an end? The arrangement by which the producers are exploited by the non-producers, the arrangement by which the producers create the wealth of the world and for creating it get a mere subsistence that keeps them from day to day. That situation is not worth continuing and it must come to an end.
Mr. G. G. McGEER (Vancouver-Burrard); I rise to speak to this bill solely with a desire to extend the very splendid presentation of facts which the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) placed before the house the other day. I know that this is not a time for careless speaking but a time when all should be prepared to extend to those charged with the heavy responsibilities of the day that measure of cooperation which they think will contribute to the success of a work that seems at last to be undertaken upon a sound and safe basis.
The bill before the house is, I believe, an attempt to deal through a national commission with the nation's gravest national problem. I may just for a moment summarize the information that was contained in the luminous statistics which the minister filed. On relief to-day there are, in round figures,
1.250.000	souls. They are divided into employables, including farmers, of 400,000, who carry, I believe, 750,000 dependents; there is an unemployable number of 50,000, carrying
100.000	dependents. The fact that there are
750.000	wives and children now dependent upon 400,000 employable Canadians who are out of work should not leave any doubt in the mind of anyone as to the nature of this problem. It is a national one. I should like, however, to approach that aspect of the issue from another angle. The men and women now unemployed constitutes a serious economic loss to the nation.
In normal times the 400,000 people out of work and now idle and on relief would be earning, on the low average of $2 a day,

working 250 days a year, some $200,000,000. That represents a wage loss per year of that amount. If we multiply that by five we find that it is a wage loss over a period of five years of one thousand million dollars. Such wages going into circulation have a turnover of at least ten times a year, so that the actual loss to the business of Canada in a five year period would be somewhere in the vicinity of ten billions of dollars. I know there is a tendency on the part of men who do not make much of a study of the general situation to think that these are large and incomprehensible figures. But when you realize that in 1929 the total volume of monetary transactions during the year measured in terms of bank cheque transactions totalled forty-eight thousand million dollars, and that in 1930 this total fell to thirty-seven thousand million, and fell again in 1935 to thirty-one thousand million, you can appreciate the fact that the loss of many billions of dollars to the trade of the Dominion of Canada must continue as long as unemployment continues.
There are other statistics that are more than significant as to the persistent downward trend of the depression. I would call the attention of the house to the fact that in 1930 the savings bank accounts of the people totalled $1,427,000,000 and the current accounts totalled $622,000,000, or a total of $2,049,000,000. In 1936, as at February, the amount of our savings accounts has increased slightly, up to $1,517,000,000, but unfortunately our current account, which is our real working account, has fallen from $622,000,000 to $533,000,000, and there is a substantial decline in the total amount of our Canadian bank deposits. These figures, which I hope are somewhat interpretative of the statistics which the minister placed before us indicate that we are far from recovery and confirm succinctly the statement made not only by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) but also by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), that the unemployment situation is a truly national problem.
In 1930, on June 13, the leader of the opposition, speaking in public, said;
I propose that parliament shall formulate a definite plan for permanent relief and that parliament as representing the people shall deal with this national problem and provide amelioration for the condition in order that next winter the Canadian people may not be facing the crisis that is upon us without having a remedy at hand.... The dominion must deal with this problem that is no longer local or provincial but affects the life of the men and women of Canada and affects the civilization of this country.... The broad problem of unemployment must be grappled with in this young country before it assumes the vast proportions that it has in England and Germany.

Employment Commission-Mr. McGeer
There should be work for every man and woman in this country. Why is there not? It is a new country, not an old country. The conditions that bring it about are entirely different to what brings it about in other countries. A new country, a vast estate, a great capital being realized.
They say the problem is a problem of the city, let the city look after it. Another says it is the province, and let the province look after them, and someone is saying the federal power should look after them....
I say to you, my fellow citizens, my fellow Canadians, speaking to the larger audiences, I am convinced this problem has now ceased to be local and provincial, and has become national in its importance. It has reached far beyond the narrow confines of Calgary or Alberta and is now stretching into the broad confines of our dominion.
Yes, and the right hon. leader of the government (Mr. Mackenzie King) on August 6, 1935, boldly acknowledged his responsibility in these words:
Unemployment of First Concern
The Liberal party believes unemployment is Canada's most urgent national problem.
Now I should like to present some facts which I believe emphasize the necessity of the national parliament assuming what both leaders have recognized is a national responsibility. That is all the more so in view of the tragedy that took place yesterday in the great province of Alberta when the government of that province was forced to acknowledge that it could not meet its obligations to bondholders because it had no money available. Addressing the annual meeting of Barclay's bank, Sir Robert Borden said:
In 1931, according to the figures recently compiled by the national committee in public finance, working under the auspices of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the total amount of income assessed by the dominion against individuals for purposes of the income tax was $815,714,684, and this was the greatest amount assessed in any year. Exemptions under the act were $3,000 for married persons and $1,500 for single persons. In 1931 the ordinary expenditure of the governments of the country, federal, provincial and municipal, totalled $920,000,000. In other words, if the governments had taken every dollar of income in excess of the moderate exemptions mentioned above, they would still be $100,000,000 short of enough money to pay their bills.
When taxation rises to the point where income is exhausted, then government is threatened with the disaster which must come from financial impotency. Let me direct the attention of the house to the fact that this condition came about under a system of so-called sound money. It developed under a system of orthodox finance; it grew into being under the defunct economy that came to us during the nineteenth century, and which will not serve to-day.
Now I want to refer to one figure that was given by the minister indicating the extent to which the national government has assumed the cost of this great problem. The dominion government had contributed 8199,000,000 since 1930. According to that statement the contribution of the dominion government was roughly $200,000,000. But that did not cover all the expenditures or obligations of the dominion government, nor did it include any of the expenditures of municipal or provincial governments. The total amount expended by way of actual expenditures and guarantees is not $200,000,000, Mr. Speaker, but something over $700,000,000. Of the amount paid out for direct relief the. dominion government has contributed about two-fifths and the municipalities and provinces about three-fifths, and the fact I want to emphasize more than anything else is that to-day from one end of the dominion to the other the municipal governments or the provincial governments, or both combined, cannot continue to carry the proportion of the burden that has been borne by the taxpayers of the junior branches of government.
I should like to read into the record a short statement given me by one of the officials of the relief section of the dominion department of labour. Let me confirm that conclusion by pointing out to you the situation that now exists in the provinces and municipalities throughout the dominion. The minister of labour for British Columbia writes me as follows:
For the fiscal year 1934-35 the gross expenditure in connection with direct relief including administration and health and other non-eontributable expenditures was $8,191,307.94, the dominion share being $2,300,196.07.... I wish to point out that during the fiscal year the dominion government paid 33 per cent of the cost in municipalities and 50 per cent in unorganized territory, from April 1 to July 31, 1934, and thereafter on a straight grant in aid basis of, $150,000 per month. It will be noted from the figures quoted for January, 1936, that the federal grant in aid is now $262,500, and also that the municipal share has been cut in half.
I asked the British Columbia provincial minister of municipal affairs to state the position of the municipalities in that province. He says that after deducting sinking fund reserves there are approximately $96,000,000 of municipal debts, with sundry other debts totalling $13,000,000. The number of municipalities that have defaulted to date is five. The amount of municipal bonds in default is

small, but the shortage in sinking funds, excluding the city of Vancouver, now totals over $15,000,000. The situation in British Columbia is no less serious than is the plight of 'Ontario. The premier of that province writes me as follows:
The last month for which complete figures are available is December, and it might be well to mention that the lists have been somewhat reduced since that time.
The total number on relief in Ontario in that month was 366,987. We estimate it at 330,000 at the present time.
The total cost of relief in December was $3,027,481, the dominion contributing, $1,050,000, the provincial government, $1,352,899, and the municipalities, $624,582. The amount of municipal debts in Ontario in 1934 was $483,934,000, or $147 per capita. The number of municipalities in default is thirty-four, and municipal debentures in default now total over $11,000,000.
In the province of Quebec the situation is much the same, with 353,000 people on relief, carrying a gross municipal debt of $578,000,000. Municipalities in that province to the number of fifty-seven are now under the direct supervision of the Quebec municipal commission.
In the province of Saskatchewan the situation is even more serious. There the total number on relief is 176,000 and the number of municipalities in default is 157.
I should like to read to the house an impartial review of the conditions which now exist. In Toronto Saturday Night of March 21 last we are told:
It is one of the paradoxes of public finance that the centres of the greatest wealth should suffer the greatest municipal poverty. Of course it is true that the largest of our cities to default (thus far) is Windsor, which stands eleventh in population in the dominion, while well over one hundred of the smaller municipalities have defaulted. Yet when we analyze the facts we find that the finances of our largest cities are in a shocking state.
But in our large cities the depression was not faced as a fact to be reckoned with. It has been consistently evaded. Toronto began in 1933 to meet its relief bill by five year loans, affording a very temporary relief to its own tax rate, which now feels the cumulative effect of three years' borrowings.
Speaking before the Canadian Club in Toronto in February, Alderman John B. Laidlaw . . . said, " Last year the chickens of the relief loans began to come home to roost to the tune of one million dollars, and they are back this year to the amount of two millions, and next year will return to the amount of nearly three millions, for we have piled up a debt of nine millions for relief payments and about wiped out our margin of borrowing powers thereby." Thus borrowing for a self-sustaining debt, or even for a productive new service, may be sound, but for a straight current expense which creates no asset, it only makes trouble.

Employment Commission-Mr. McGeer
The city of Montreal is in an even worse plight. I wish now to place before you, Mr. Speaker, a very sound report which was made by Professor Goldenberg of McGill university to the mayors' conference which recently met in Ottawa. I may also add that the figures that came to this house through the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) were first compiled by provincial governments at the request of the mayors' conference in 1935 acting under the direction of Professor Marsh, also of McGill university, which has made a substantial contribution to our better understanding of this problem by indicating the need for the compilation of these facts. Professor Goldenberg's report has been very succinctly summarized by the editor of the Ottawa .Citizen and I should like to put a part of that summary on record:
Three important points were established by Professor II. Carl Goldenberg of McGill in his survey of municipal finances for the dominion conference of mayors, tabled on the opening day of that gathering. They were (1) that in the last five years there has been a great decline in the assessed and market value of real property which is the main source of municipal revenue, (2) that this decline in value had been accompanied by a general increase in civic tax rates, but (3) that the increase in the tax rate has not necessarily increased revenue while it has heavily increased tax arrears.
With respect to taxable assessment, Professor Goldenberg produced figures showing that it had dropped by $259,000,000 in Quebec municipalities, $115,000,000 in Ontario municipalities, and by corresponding amounts in other provinces.
And cryptically, but with clear and final definiteness, he said that unless some wholesale measure of relief is extended to municipal government throughout the Dominion of Canada, many of our Canadian municipalities cannot escape bankruptcy.
Let me say that municipal taxation constitutes the most definite repudiation of obligations representing the investment of Canadian wealth in real estate subject to the taxation powers of municipal government. We have wiped out accumulative wealth having an assessed value of $8,500,000,000. Holdings of improved property in the majority of Canadian cities have changed from an asset to a liability. We cannot go on with this disastrous imposition of taxation without meeting disaster. Let me indicate what the city council is doing in a desperate and impossible attempt to meet the situation in Montreal. Montreal's gross funded debt amounts to $268,842,000, and its annual tax levy to $34,000,000, more than half of which, $16,778,000, goes to pay debt charges. These terrifying taxes are now threatened: a $5 tax on all automobiles in the city; from $75 to
$250 a year on trucks; $10 on every dance held elsewhere than in a licensed dance hall or private home; $10 a year for each "no parking" sign; $25 a year for every parking ground; $200 a year on every building or lot used for the sale or exchange of automobiles; $100 a year on '.very person conducting a trucking business and $10 a year on each employee; $2 on every employee of a butcher, baker, pastry baker or grocer; 25 cents on every new piece of plumbing installed in every building, the certificate of inspection to be issued only after payment of the tax. Then there is a special tax, the amount of which has yet to be decided, on every hotel and boarding house in the city; a $200 annual tax on laundries, private hospitals and second hand stores; a special tax of $200 on all solicitors for the sale of goods, and a $100 tax on all jobbers. There is a tax of $500 on theatres and concert halls, plus 85 cents for each seat; $500 tax on dance halls; $50 tax on museums or other amusement halls; $1,000 tax on night clubs, cafes concerts, cafes dansants, and so on; $200 tax on every one canvassing for orders for photographs or doing photographic business elsewhere than in a regular business establishment; a tax of SI per square inch on advertising placards and posters, whether on private property or not. Then, there is a tax on automobile licences not exceeding one-third of the cost of such licence. This resort to desperate taxation methods shows that municipal governments cannot even with provincial governments carry three-fifths of what is acknowledged to be a national responsibility.
Let me now give some information as to the actual revenue position of a city with which I am conversant. The report I have in my hand was made by a group of business men the most responsible I could gather together in the city of Vancouver. Their report to our city council in part was as follows:
The situation is growing more and more acute owing to present methods of taxation. If we are ever to meet our obligations we must work out a more just and equitable distribution of the cost of municipal government, in order to restore property values.
In support of the contention that the present system of assessment and taxes is inequitable and confiscatory, and that it thoroughly destroys property values and the taxpayers' equity, an economic analysis was made of a large number of properties in the business section of the city. This survey, covering 111 properties, disclosed the following facts:
1.	That the taxes had increased between the years 1928 and 1934 by 42-6 per cent.
2.	That the gross revenue had decreased by 44-8 per cent.

Employment Commission-Mr. McGeer
And, that the value of property, measured in terms of income, had fallen by 92-1 per cent.
The province of British Columbia cannot help the city of Vancouver because its troubles are just as grave and acute as is the other's. In Alberta, with default now a fact, its provincial debt of $179,000,000, and the municipal debt is proportionately large, is now in jeopardy. In the province of British Columbia municipal and provincial debts together amount to over $425,000,000, to-day neither British Columbia nor Alberta can relieve the municipalities of their obligations, because the sources of revenue available and left by the national parliament to the provinces are not sufficient to permit the financing and maintenance of peace, order and good government in the provinces.
May I for a moment refer to the observation of others who have considered it the responsibility of this parliament to maintain a taxation and financial system that will permit provincial and municipal governments to carry on upon that issue. Hon. A. T. Galt during the confederation debates said:
The 80 cents per head which it is proposed to allow the local government out of the general exchequer for the purpose of meeting their local expenditures, these local expenditures include such items as the administration of justice, the support of education, grants to literary and scientific societies, hospitals and charities, and such other matters as cannot be regarded as devolving upon the general government. The fact that it is contemplated to give a subsidy of 80 cents per head to each of the provinces, in transferring to the general government all the larger sources of revenue, and placing in their hands, with a single exception-that of direct taxation-all the amounts whereby the expenditure of the people may be made to contribute to the wants of the state, it must be evident to every one that some portion of the resources thus placed at the disposal of the general government must in some form or other be available to supply the hiatus that otherwise takes place between the sources of local revenue and the demands of local expenditure.
Then, Sir Charles Tupper in the House of Commons on June 11, 1869, acknowledged the same thing in somewhat wider terms when he said that after confederation had been accomplished it was intended to have provincial and federal commissions set up to make an exhaustive inquiry into the needs of the provinces. After this inquiry had been completed it was intended to make a just and final settlement. Dealing with the power to alter the settlement of 1867 and to change the British North America Act he said he did not think that the house was prepared to assert the principle, under any circumstances, that it was not in a position to give any fair

consideration which any province ought to receive, or to extend it any relief beyond what the Union Act provided.
_ Sir Thomas White, in dealing with the question of the right of the federal parliament to invade the field of direct taxation with an income tax, said:
The dominion government under the provisions of the North America Act is empowered to raise revenue by any mode or form of taxation, whether direct or indirect; on the contrary, the provinces, and by consequence the municipalities which derive their taxation power from the provinces, are confined in the raising of revenues to the measures of direct taxation. For this reason, since the outbreak of the war, I have hesitated to bring down a measure of federal income taxation, and I have not regarded it as expedient, except in case of manifest public necessity, such as I believe exists at the present time, that the dominion should invade the field to which the provinces are solely confined for the raising of their revenue.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier was not indifferent to this great issue. Speaking in the House of Commons in 1907 he said:
Lower Canada would not have entered confederation if as a consequence she had been obliged to resort to direct taxation to levy the revenues necessary to carry on her domestic affairs.... It is not to be wondered at that when the provinces represented at that conference agreed to surrender to the central government the exclusive right of taxation in way of customs and excise they should at the same time have stipulated as a condition precedent that a certain portion of the revenue that is collected should be returned to them, and a portion sufficient to permit them without having recourse to direct taxation to carry on their provincial affairs. This is the reason of the enactment which we have before us in the sixty-fourth resolution of the Quebec conference. It was one of the many promises which had to be made in order to render confederation possible, and without which possibly confederation would have remained a dream.
Those words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier echo strangely in this house-that the federal parliament had no right to exhaust sources of revenue necessary to maintain provincial and municipal government. The guiding wisdom of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, sir, is available to us to-day and we should follow it without delay.
I should like to answer from another authority a statement which I think has been too often made with carelessness, and indifference to the truth. It is that the Dominion of Canada has weathered the storm as well as any other nation. This is not the conclusion of competent and unbiased authority. On January 18 of this year the Economist of London published one of the most complete reviews of the Dominion of Canada, its resources and its future possibilities, I have ever had the privilege of reading. Summariz-

Employment Commission-Mr. McGeer
ing our present plight it makes this statement :
The political experts do not concede any future for the reconstruction party as a separate unit, and the impression prevails that within four years the disillusioned voters of Alberta will be ready to turn and rend Mr. Aberhart and his lieutenants. The chances are that the reconstructionists and the social credit voters will drift into the C.C.F. camp.

In the new parliament the C.C.F. will only have eight representatives-
My friends groan now, but if that takes place they may groan even louder. I continue :
*-but if they can develop some debating strength, and if the government's plans for solving the unemployment and other problems go awry, their case for a wholesale reconstruction of Canada's economy will get a hearing in the country.
Within the ranks of the C.C.F. are a large number of the younger intelligentsia of Canada, some of whom have just produced a very interesting book entitled Social Planning for Canada, which exposes in succinct and forceful style the weaknesses of the present economic system and propounds a concrete plan for its reformation on socialist lines. Some of their proposals are beyond the range of practical politics in Canada for many a long day, but at least their party puts before the electorate a definite program. In a country where there are still a million and quarter people on public relief, and where a large element of the farming community is in sore straits, with debt burdens pressing heavily upon it, such a program will have an increasing appeal unless the Liberal ministry can open the road to recovery of real and permanent prosperity. The question many people in Canada are asking to-day is why the economic life of a country, which has such vast and varied resources, cannot be so organized as to provide a reasonable sustenance for 101 millions of people, when Sweden, another country in northern latitudes with a much smaller area and little first-class land, manages to support 7,000,000 people without condemning any large proportion of them to serious privation.
It is a reflection upon the government of this nation that the Economist of London, viewing Sweden on the one hand and Canada on the other, can offer such a reflection, and it does not confirm the conclusion that we have weathered the depression better than other countries. The Economist then goes on to say:
The social, political and economic problems facing the new Liberal government of Mr. Mackenzie King are scarcely less acute or less preemptory than those facing President Roosevelt. What are these immediate problems?
The urban population of the dominion is now greater, though not much greater, than the rural; but some of the western wheat provinces are, in Mr. Bennett's words, "bankrupt."
There are grave Canadian social problems. The drift of agricultural unemployed to the towns (which may account for some of the "rise" in the urban populations); the entirely separate enclave of French Canadians, with their own language, religion, law and education system, and with their differentially higher rate of natural increase; the return of former Canadian emigrants from the United States; the stabilization of the population by damping down fresh immigration; the political and social evidences of something approaching despair in the western provinces; all these problems have to be tackled, and the revelations of the price spreads commission that "trade abuses" existed on a very large scale in Canada are likely to provide plenty of opportunities to reformers for some time to come.
Finally, there is the entire complex of financial problems; the bankruptcy of the western provinces; the piling up of new debt by the federal government; the delay in attaching the rate of interest on these debts; the problem of the two railway systems and their deficits; the absence of organized nation wide unemployment relief (there were 1,100,000 persons dependent on some form of public relief last November, out of just over 10 millions); and the problematical cost of the measures to help farmers.
All these problems must be attacked and solved to bring this dominion back to prosperity. But we have this word of hope from the same survey:
The new brooms with which Canada's new premier has surrounded himself may soon be seen sweeping away much of the debris left by the impact of world wide depression upon an ill prepared dominion. Meanwhile, the special review of Canada which we offer to our readers this week should help them to gauge the significance of Canada's problems, as well as the magnitude of her possibilities. For, if the many articles contributed by Canadian and English authorities to that survey reveal one thing more clearly than any other, it is that Canada's opportunities far surpass her immediate problems. It is no belittlement of her development hitherto if we say that she remains a land rather of promise than of achievement. All those who read our review will realize how fair is that promise; and they will wish her well.
Clearly, Mr. Speaker, we can and should charge the deplorable conditions in the Dominion of Canada to bad government and to nothing else. There is nothing wrong with our people; there is nothing wrong with the vast heritage of wealth that is ours. There is no reason why we cannot do far more than we are doing, and moreover, we need in the government not supermen but just men who will use the rules of plain reason and common sense.
I should like now to submit a short summary on which I appealed to the electorate in Vancouver.
