speechtext:
This is the summary, Mr. Speaker.
We are far from secure, and whether or not our western civilization can survive the present depression is still open to question. We are at the parting of the ways. The day has arrived when progress through exploitation must give way to progress through order, sustained by government control and regulation. This great change must be brought about by constitutional reform, or we are bound to suffer the chaos of revolution which will end in dictatorship with little or no benefit to the masses.
We are at the parting of the ways in the course we must take.
Humanity must have a better deal than the private money system has provided.
Real wealth must be created and distributed to satisfy the needs of human progress and individual contentment.
The desire for interest and profit must not be allowed to prevent available and realizable supply from satisfying the demands of humanity for the necessities, comforts and conveniences of life.
The wages of men must be placed above the wages of money.
Consumers and taxpayers must be supplied with the means of buying the goods and services available and of paying taxes that are levied.
Unemployment due to technological advancements must be balanced by employment in public works and the advancement of social service. Seasonal unemployment must be guarded against.
The standard of living in agricultural community and city, of those employed in public and private activity and of those engaged in domestic and foreign trade, must be balanced. Destitution must be eliminated and consumers' buying power must be sustained. Highways, railways, airways and communication facilities, buildings for administration, national defence, law enforcement, education, health, entertainment and other public service, and the improvement of the appearance of both city and country, must be undertaken. Parks and playgrounds must be developed, and natural resources must be conserved.
Children denied the right of work under child labour laws must be cared for. Proper pensions, superannuation and other allowances must be provided for mothers, for the sick, the injured, the veterans, and those who, through the passing years, are no longer able to sustain themselves; and age in years should not be the arbitrary governing factor.

The taxpayer must be relieved from the existing unpayable debt load.
The advancement of education, health, law enforcement and good government must be carried on.
How can this be accomplished? Not under the old financial structure, Mr. Speaker, but through a commission such as this bill contemplates, examining the whole problem in all its phases, and helping to bring about a spirit of cooperation between the government and finance and industry and commerce, with the people at large willing to cooperate and help this country move forward as we ought to be able to move if we all work together, creating for each other's use, distributing for each other's benefit, and making the life of every Canadian what it should be under the blessed heritage that we enjoy in every part of this great and broad dominion.
I congratulate the minister upon his presentation of the bill and his conception of the work, and the government upon the undertaking, and my hope is that when it comes to the supplementary estimates the Minister of Finance will be as broad and liberal in his conception of what is to be done as the Minister of Labour has been.

subsubtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOR NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
In rising to discuss the proposed commission set-up, I want first of all to commend the Minister of Labour (Mr.-Rogers) upon the broad way he travelled and the area that he covered. I recognize that he, like the party in power, is faced with a gigantic task in endeavouring to solve the problem of unemployment that has persisted so long in Canada. I feel, however, that this problem does not belong to the labour department or to any one particular department. As I understand the bill, it is to provide for a commission whose duties shall be to provide for a national registration and classification in cooperation with the provinces, to determine the conditions to be complied with by any province obtaining grants for relief from the government of Canada, to investigate relief abuses, and so forth.
In the first place, Mr. Speaker, I do not believe it is the duty of the government to find employment. I do believe, however, it is the duty of the government entirely to eliminate poverty, but as I recognize that we are in a transitional period, we have to move more or less along orthodox lines and say that the only way that our people can live is to provide employment for them so that they may receive wages. I think one of the greatest parts if not the greatest part of

Employment Commission-Mr. Poole
our problem is that affecting the youth of this country. In the past few years we have seen many interesting experiments in this connection, not so much in Canada as in Great Britain and the United States. I have here a copy of a statement dealing with the work of the National Youth Administration in the United States:
The National Youth Administration admits that it is all but appalled before the problems of unoccupied youth. Of the $50,000,000 set aside by the federal government about one-half is being used to help 300,000 college and high school students to continue their studies, 31,000 of these being in New York state. The question is how to help the remaining 5,000,000 or 6,000,000 unemployed young persons, particularly the half million between 16 and 25 who have finished school and never yet have had a job that paid them wages. Aubrey Williams, executive director of the National Youth Administration, gives his findings in a startling statement-"Millions of young persons seem to be denied the right to work and earn their own food."
Mr. Williams and his assistants hopefully set out to find jobs for young Americans, but halted before the discovery that there were not jobs enough to serve even the men with families.
Only yesterday one hon. member on the government benches told us of 400 applicants for seventeen jobs. The only way in which we differ from the United States is in degree, but we can see all around us evidence that ours is an identical problem. I continue:
There was hopeful talk of developing apprenticeships, but when a trade was selected for a beginning, it was found 60 per cent of the qualified operatives in that trade were unemployed. Again, an unhappy halt. Then came the forced conclusion that at no time now in sight would private industry be able to absorb these willing young would-be workers. The work survey turns reluctantly to some kind of public project, something for cultural expansion and increasing of natural resources-What kind of a generation is this that says it cannot absorb its young?
Director Williams wonders whether society will have to be made over for the accommodation of youth. His group studies the possi-bilties of gymnasiums and church and school auditoriums being used for some general program to occupy youth's time. But this would not meet the real need. It would not afford youth its sublime right to hardships and victories. The nation must face its grave duty of saving youth by putting it to work, seasoning it, testing it unto full development. More spiritual insight is required in discovering the surely right way. This generation not merely needs its youth; it cannot move forward without the help of its youth. To cry that the country has no actual need of its youth would be the admission of utter calamity-It would be a false claim that the nation has no to-morrow.
I believe that those words, discussing the National Youth Administration in the United States, somehow measure the difficulty which
our own Minister of Labour will meet in trying to carry out his program.
Again, it has been clearly indicated by the government, and particularly by the Minister of Labour, that the government cannot continue to spend money, that we must look to cooperation from private industry. It will be a wonderful day if and when we get cooperation from private industry. We look at the report of the price spreads commission and find that even here, in the capital city of Canada, major industries are being subsidized by local governments, industries that have as many as twenty-five salesmen on their staff who are not paid a nickel beyond commissions and are forced to knock at the door of the relief offices of this city to get a living. That state of things is true not only of this city but of western Canada, in connection with industries that have assets to the tune of hundreds of millions of dollars. Though the leaders of these industries sometimes parade their faith in Canada, industry of this kind can best be described as business without a soul, big business chisellers, people who care nothing for the future of this country. It is these people who are always pressing the municipalities for reduced assessments to throw the burden on small property owners.
Turning for a moment to the address given by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), I understand the difficulties he faces, and I agree with him in many things. He said:
There is another consideration which musl also be kept in mind as we approach the problem of unemployment and relief in its social aspect. I have suggested that a sufficiency of food and shelter, clothing and medical attention must be provided for those in need.
That is true. There is no person in this house, no person in this dominion who could put forward an intelligent argument why the people of Canada should not receive not only the bare necessities of life but life in abundance. We have the physical goods; our low standard of living to-day exists only because there is something else lacking-not goods, but finances.
I was struck yesterday by the remark of an hon. member that governments should not interfere with business. Others say the trouble is that we have too much machinery, that by its use we are depriving people of employment, the inference, being, of course, that we should not use so much of it. But I turn to the front page of the Ottawa Citizen to-day and I find this-and it is the act of a government that is trying to find employment:
Finance department work in the branch of the comptroller of the treasury performed by thirty-one employees and seven business machines on rental at $810 per month would require 65 persons without machines, Hon.

Employment Commission-Mr. Poole
C. A. Dunning, finance minister, informed Ralph Maybank, Liberal, Winnipeg South Centre, in the House of Commons yesterday.
It was explained that since 1933 the finance department has rented three punching machines, two tabulators, one sorter and one reproducing punch from a Toronto business machine company. The machines are installed at the central pay office and are used in the preparation of the payrolls and the writing of cheques for 35,000 government employees and for the annuitants under the Government Annuities Act, approximately 54,000 cheques being issued monthly.
This is the point I am trying to make. While the government persistently refuses to realize that it is due to the advancement of science that we have so many unemployed in the country, the administration is endeavouring to find employment for our people and at the same time displacing man power, and of course wages, by the introduction of machines into departments. What is true in that instance is true in connection with all industry in this country. Many people in Canada and in the House of Commons cry to high heaven because we have so many unemployed, and they take the number of the unemployed as the measure of our national poverty. But to the man who has given any serious consideration to the science of production and distribution and to the purpose of an economic system it must surely be evident that every unemployed man in the country is a measure of our scientific advancement. The purpose of an economic system is to reduce toil, to produce more goods and to distribute them, and the problem in Canada to-day is therefore not one of employment. Employment is but a means to an end, not an end in itself. The difficulty lies in the fact that we recognize only one means by which people can live, and that is through the system of wages, and the system of wages has broken down because our financial structure will not permit the people to receive the means whereby we can distribute the goods.
The Minister of Labour tells us that it would ' cost between 1300,000,000 and $400,000,000 to put to work the employables in Canada. In other words, the only way in which in this dominion we can feed, clothe and shelter our own people is by going into debt, placing a chattel mortgage on the future, and increasing the burden of debt on Canadian generations yet unborn. But perhaps there is something that we have overlooked-I must not forget that-because the Minister of Labour quoted an authority of 1842, Thomas Carlyle. He told us yesterday that Carlyle said there was very little hope; he struck quite a pessimistic note.

I would remind the minister that the conditions under which people lived in 1842 were vastly different from the conditions under which we live to-day. At that time the world was expanding; world capitalism was building up and there was a place for surplus products. But to-day we have reached the stage where we can expand no more, where every nation is indulging in economic nationalism, endeavouring to produce its own goods independently of other nations. For evidence of that we have only to turn to a statement made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). The basic industry of the country is agriculture, and this is what the leader of the opposition has said, as reported at page 1611 of Hansard. He quotes first what he said in the house in 1935:
Mr. Bennett: The hon. member will see as I proceed. The average production of Europe (ex Russia) for the period 1923-24 to 1927-28 was 1,240,000,000 bushels. The average importations by importing countries for the same period were 601,000,000 bushels. The average consumption by European countries was
1.841.000.	000 bushels. It will be observed that you have an average consumption during that period of 1,841,000,000 bushels. It has been stated that there has been a diminution in consumption but I give these figures to show that such is not the case. For the period 1929-30 to 1933-34-these are the crop years ending July 31-the average production of Europe (ex Russia) was 1,496,000,000 bushels. The average imports by importing countries for the same period had fallen from 601,000,000 bushels to 469,000,000 bushels while the average consumption had risen to 1,965,000,000 from
1.841.000.	000 bushels. I come now to the last crop year, 1933-34. The European production for that year was 1,749,000,000 bushels while for this year the imports had fallen to
374.000.	000 bushels. I ask the house to note that the average imports for 1923-24 to 1927-28 were 601,000,000 bushels and these had fallen to 469,000,000 bushels for the period 1929-30 to 1933-34, there being a further decrease to
374.000.	000 bushels for the last crop year. In this last year the total consumption had risen to the largest figure in history, 2,123,000,000 bushels.
Then he makes this comment:
I stated then, as I state now, that there was an erroneous opinion abroad and in many sections of our country as well, that the people were consuming less wheat. The figures issued from Rome, and the figures issued as well by the wheat committee to which I shall presently refer, indicate that that was not the case and that consumption rose to the highest figure we have record of in history, namely,
2.123.000.	000 bushels by the countries to which I referred last year.
This is the point. If we are depending upon absorbing our unemployed into industry by means of the export of wheat to the nations of the world on the basis on which we did this in days gone by, then there

Employment Commission-Mr. Poole
is little hope. Surely the figures are a good enough measuring stick, and if there is no hope from that source what then has the government to offer? The commission which has been suggested might give better administration, but it cannot feed more people; that requires something different from anything we have been given. I believe I can call in evidence Premier Bracken of Manitoba, who has estimated that during the first four years of the depression the purchasing power of the western farmers was reduced by an average of $450,000,000 a year. Hon. members know only too well how that has contributed to the unemployment of industrial workers in eastern Canada.
The problem that faces the people of Canada to-day is not one of unemployment but one of finance, and that is where we must focus our attention. It can be best described as a financial stone wall against which governments, business, agriculture and labour forces are running their deluded heads in an attempt to end the depression.
Before a commission or anyone else can deal with the problem that confronts this countiy, we must rid ourselves of many of the misconceptions which we have inherited from the middle ages. In the first place, we have heard for five years that there is a depression. I do not know what is meant by that, but the implication is that we are short of something, and yet I do not know of anything that we are short of, anything that we could not produce. If there is anything that we have not, we have the available man power to produce it. It is quite true that we had depressions in 1842, when we could not produce enough, but to-day, in 1936, with approximately a million Canadians enjoying a standard of living that can be compared only with that of a Chinese coolie, the only excuse is that we can produce so much; that the wage system has broken down and that machines have taken the places of these men. Again, they tell us that we cannot produce enough; I remember quite clearly that this was another statement made by members of the Liberal party in the last provincial election campaign in Alberta. When you asked them why there were so many unemployed, they could not reconcile the two statements. Every man in this country is potential wealth, available man power to process the natural resources of Canada so that the people may use them. So this commission is faced with this impossible task of trying to end unemployment with foreign markets gone. They have been obliterated; they can be obtained no longer, unless of course a state of war should be declared in Europe.
There are only two proposals that can be made by this commission. If they wish to find employment for the employables they can do so only by increasing taxation and at the same time reducing the standard of living of others or by borrowing more money, in other words increasing our national debt. I do not want to discuss money too much, because the last time I did so one hon. member took exception, but I want to say this: The hon. member for Yancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) suggested that the people of Alberta would tear the premier of that province to pieces because of the promises he had made and had not fulfilled. I want to say that I believe the wish was father to the thought. In my opinion we in that province have the only solution that is before the Canadian people to-day. If anyone else has another solution we are still waiting to heai it. We do know you will not solve the problem by going into debt. We know you wil. not solve it through a loan council, by centralizing the powers of finance. We know you will never increase the prosperity of Canada or of its people if you depend upon the exportation of Canadian goods. We shall export goods from this country in any great volume only when we use our wheat as purchasing power instead of going into the markets of the world to sell.
We must concentrate our attention upon the real problem that confronts Canada, instead of always suggesting palliatives, commissions, committees, unemployment relief programs and so on. We may well criticize big business because of the crimes it has committed against the Canadian public, who were awakened to the situation only through the evidence given before the price spreads commission last year, but there is another business whose crimes will never be known. I refer to finance, the people who have the power to make money, the people who control prices, the people whom, so far, this government has refused to touch. I had some hope that the government would bring about some monetary reform, but after listening to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) digging himself in and imposing certain conditions upon provinces before they could obtain a dominion guarantee, it seems to me that the minister is looking forward to many years during which we shall have to keep on borrowing. If the government were sincere in their program of monetary reform we would not need a loan council, because we would strip the financial monopoly of the power they have and return it to the people. But do not touch them; criticize anyone else,



Employment Commission

Mr. Poole
chisel on the blind people of Canada, the exservice men, the incapacitated and the widows, but do not touch the bankers. I am firmly convinced that the people of Canada should understand that this money game is the biggest racket that was ever perpetrated upon any people; that money is just made, that it is based upon something belonging to the Canadian people, not to the bankers, and that the man who controls it controls the economic life and destiny of every man, woman and child within the borders of this dominion. It is useless for us to discuss setting up commissions or trying to find employment by cooperating with industry; this is all so much ballyhoo. That will be so until such time as we obtain the key that opens the door to prosperity, until we say to the bankers: You have ruled long enough; the time has come when you may no longer indulge in usury. That will be so until we take over the control of finance and issue it, first to the consumer, recognizing as we do that the purpose of our economic society is to increase the standard of living of the individual by increasing production and making these goods available.
I do not know what the near future may hold, but I do know that future generations in Canada will look upon us with rather mixed feelings when they see the five years that have been lost by one generation; when they see that we sacrificed everything, education, ambition, initiative, even our public buildings and highways, because we refused to do the one thing that was necessary, because we were afraid to attack the citadel of finance for fear of political suicide. But I say, that before we can have one jot of prosperity of any kind we must take over the control of finance and change our policy. We must make money available to production for the purposes of production. You have to make available to the consumer a national dividend. The purpose of that national dividend is to monetize the goods which are piled up to-day and which cannot be bought because of the difference between cost and price. Of course that cannot be done yet because we have not so far recognized that the only purpose of the machine is to produce goods, and the only value of those gods is ultimate consumption. So many things could be said, so much evidence could be piled up against this foolish system under which we are living that one could deal with the question for forty-eight hours and still leave many things unsaid. But there is one interesting thing I have noticed this session. I have been waiting very patiently for someone to defend the present financial system and I have yet to hear

this done. I have yet to hear anyone suggest how we can put our people to work without increasing our debt. I have yet to hear anyone tell us how we can increase our exports of goods in a wTorld in which each nation is trying to become self-sufficient.
So, to sum up, we are to have a commission created, and the best it will have accomplished five years from now-and I say this not to criticize the Minister of Labour because I am quite convinced of his ability and sincerity but I know he has a gigantic task ahead of him-will be possibly a better and more efficient administration of relief. There is one point I am afraid of in regard to the commission. At the present time in the municipalities and the provinces the relief recipient has an opportunity to go directly to the local authorities and plead his case if he things he is not getting justice.^ Now, a commission is to be set up which will take away that opportunity and make it very hard for the' mass of the people to place their case before those in control, because a commission is so unapproachable. I trust that when this commission is set up it will not take away from the municipalities the right to fix the scale of relief, or interfere with them in any way whatsoever.
It seems that we are going to wait for another year to find out what effect the policy of the present government will have on unemployment in this country. I believe it is the wish of this little group in this corner not to put any obstacle in the way of the government but to help and cooperate with them to have this legislation passed as expeditiously as possible so that the Canadian people may have an opportunity at an early date to see that what is required to bring about prosperity in Canada, is not commissions, not export markets, not an extensive scheme of public works which will increase our national debt, but a major operation, nothing short of changing our financial policy, taking it from the control of a monopoly and making available to the people at all times sufficient purchasing power to enable them to purchase the total price values. We must recognize that the purpose of an economic system is to produce the maximum of goods with the minimum of effort, and the purpose of the machine, which is an inheritance left to us by generations long since gone, is to make available to mankind in abundance the natural resources of the world, to make life more abundant. It was created for that purpose. We bemoan as a national calamity the fact that we have the machine. Surely it must be evident to any schoolboy that the purpose of a machine system and of science is to de-

Employment Commission-Mr. MacNicol
prive men of employment. I do not mean by that that men will be idle in the total sense of the word; I mean the removal from society of wage slavery, compelling men to go into factories and workshops to do jobs that they absolutely hate.
I am convinced that the only obstacles in our way are those people who have the traditional view that if work is not found for people they will be demoralized. The surprising thing is the acceptance of the statement that men will always have to work. I hope that in a short time they will cease to work long hours in factories and in industry. There are all kinds of creative work that men will always find to do, because man is a creative creature, but the fact that we have machines that * will produce so much is no reason why the people of Canada, the youth of Canada, should be sacrificed in order to leave intact one portion of our mediaeval system which is of no use in the modern age. It has to be removed. I make this prophecy. I speak of something that I utterly believe. I was not elected to the House of Commons because I belonged to a party; I think one of the curses of our modern society is partyism, but I have for some three years lectured on this subject, and given some years of study to analyzing our present system, and I say this, that we are in a rapidly moving age, the most rapid movement of any period in the world's history, and we are on the threshhold of something. We are living in a day when we must make decisions, not decisions that will affect us for only a day or a month or a year, but decisions that will affect the national life of this country and affect world policy.
I believe that this government will solve this problem when they focus their attention on money, remembering always that the banker bases his credit, that with which we do ninety-five per cent of the business of Canada, upon the ability of the people of Canada to make available the natural resources of the country for the needs of the people. It is on this basis that we should issue our national credit, for the purpose of controlling prices, because it is a well known fact that the man who controls the volume of money, controls prices, and the man who controls prices controls the economic life of the people.
What chance has the farmer? In 1928 he thought he was living.in a day of prosperity. He was living in a period of inflation, that is all, when the bankers made bank credit available for production. People were working then; this epidemic of laziness had not struck us; people at that time thought they were part of the nation. In 1929 the crash came.
Nothing happened really, only that the bankers reversed their policy and began to deflate. Listen to Premier Bracken again. This is a Liberal speaking:
Premier Bracken of Manitoba has estimated that during the first four years of the depression the purchasing power of western farmers was reduced by an average of $450,000,000 per year.
There is the trouble-lack of purchasing power. You have goods up here and purchasing power down here. Of course we get exactly the same thing as they got in the United States. In that country they carried on an experiment under which they began to reduce the volume of goods and to equate existing purchasing power, while 18,000,000 people rambled through their streets. We can do exactly the same thing, and the results would be identical, or we can do something else. We could increase the volume of purchasing power so that it would equal the volume or height of price values. Of course I know the cry that will go up; people will say that we should have inflation. First, we should have reflation-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after a careful rereading of Bill No. 14, which, I admit frankly, was prepared with the best hopes of providing employment for the unemployed, and after rereading the minister's speech on moving second reading I regret that I find very little, if anything, which could give reasonably prompt realization to the hopes of thousands of unemployed looking for jobs. I am afraid the unemployed have looked for too much from the academic experience of the minister. Theories are all right, perhaps, when propounded behind the ivy clad walls of some scholastic hall, but a problem such as this requires much more than theories. It requires a lot of vigour, action and practical knowledge to take care of employment, in times such as these.
The needs of the unemployed are so great that I only wish I could say something to encourage the minister in the belief that his proposal to form a commission will be a panacea for the difficulties of the unemployed. I regret that I cannot do this. For a few moments I should like to deal with a few of the statements made by other hon. members, but unless time permits I shall confine my observations to some statements of the minister.
The minister's speech made some days ago I have boiled down to four main statements: (a) that the lowest index of unemployment was at March 1, 1933, when it stood at 76-9 per
1726	COMMONS
Employment Commission-Mr. MacNicol
cent as compared with the 1926 index, taken at 100; (b) that improvement from March 1, 1933, to March 1, 1936, rose to 98 per cent plus, or an improvement of 28J per cent; (c) that the problem is still critical and acute, and (d) that a national employment commission is in the opinion of the minister, and perhaps in that of the government too, the way out of the impasse in which the country now finds itself.
I should like to divide (d) into four separate headings: (1) that through the commission it is expected that the originating of employment will take place by offering in a large measure advice and plans to industry; (2) the planning of long-range measures; (3) the registering and tabulation of unemployed, and (4) the elimination of certain companies or shops which give unfair and excessively low wages.
Dealing first with division (d), namely the hope that the commission, committee or council may do effective work, may I say that under this division we find nothing new. Many years ago Bismarck made the same suggestion, and when the present German constitution was framed at Weimar in 1919 a clause of the constitution enacts just that. It did not last long. They established a committee, council or commission of 326 members covering all classes of business, labour, financial and other classes of which the German nation is formed. But it was found unsatisfactory. The excessive cost, the duplication and the delay made it impossible of action.
Other European states followed in the path of Germany. Poland, Spain, Portugal and France all tried out similar plans and each one discarded the plan as top-heavy, costly, slow and ineffective. Under its referendum No. 58 the United States prepared a somewhat similar plan which has since been abandoned. Great Britain, however, did not adopt that procedure. Under its Department of Labour Great Britain was divided into seven employment districts, which in turn were divided into 1,128 subdistricts, and I believe through their plan they have accomplished something. At least they are in touch with the situation in all parts of the country, and have been making an honest effort to transfer unwanted labour in one part of the country to meet the labour requirements in another. May I tell the minister and through him the government that to-day we have heard a lot about industry. I was connected with industry for many years, but I shall not attempt to reply to the statements which have been made. After all, in many respects it is like other vocations. If you are going to be a medical practitioner you must know something about

medical practice. If you are going to be a lawyer you must know something about law. There are too many who think they know all about industry, but who actually know little whatever about it. To-day industry has been throttled and crucified by the overwhelming cost of government in Canada. What have we? We have one federal government, nine provincial governments, four thousand municipal governments and twenty-four thousand boards of education. Each one inflicts taxation upon industry, and upon everything else which goes to make up business in Canada.
In addition to this tremendous and terrific overhead of cost it is proposed to add another commission. To what? To the fifty-eight commissions which we already have. The other day when on the introduction of the bill I said that the country was being commissioned to death, and overgoverned to death, I received many letters from all parts of the country asking me when I spoke again to give the list of commissions, and I now propose to do that. ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOR NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to support this bill in the hope that some good will come of it. It is said that unemployment is Canada's greatest problem, but I submit that our greatest problem is the abolition of poverty, and that is mainly a question of finance. Control of credit means control of money; control of money means control of prices; the control of prices means control of profits and profits control wages and salaries. To abolish poverty we need to consume to the limits of our desires or our powers to produce. Is this financially possible? I submit that it is, because it was possible during the war. If it was possible during the war it is possible in times of peace.
Is it financially desirable? I submit that that is a question for the people of Canada to decide. The people demand an end to the scandal of poverty in the midst of plenty. If the financier will do his part the people will do theirs; if the financier will not do his part, or if he says he cannot, then he must be replaced by those who can and will. That is the duty of the government of Canada.
Mr. A. J. LAPOINTE (Matapedia-Ma-tane); Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words in English before continuing in French, on the first occasion that I have an opportunity to speak in this house. As a
1732	COMMONS
Employment Commission-Mr. Lapointe (Matane)
new member I realize it takes courage to address this chamber, but as I have been told that the experienced members are very indulgent to newcomers, I feel more at ease.
First, I wish to commend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) for the great speech he made the other day in moving the second reading of the bill to create a national employment commission. Although I quite agree that already we have too many commissions, I sincerely believe that this commission will be of great benefit to our country.
We have often been told in this house that the Canadian people placed great confidence in the Liberal party at the last general election. This is true; we quite realize it, and we want to prove that we are worthy of such confidence, to show that we are ready and willing to face the situation, difficult as it is, and to do our utmost to bring back prosperity and happiness in the numerous homes darkened so long with the shadow of unemployment, suffering and distress. I know that the task is not an easy one, but we must show that the faith of our country in this government is going to be justified during the next five years.
(Translation): Mr. Speaker, I now wish to contiue my observations in the French language.
More than six years ago, at a time when the present crisis began to sap the economical structure of the world, no one could have foreseen that to-day we would still be confronted with the same difficulties and endeavouring to solve the same vexing problems. It is obvious that the situation remains most uncertain. After more than six years of waiting, thousands and thousands of men still go out in search of employment only to return, disappointed, weary and almost desperate, to homes without food and children half naked.
I do not propose to indulge in mere declamation. I know full well that I am repeating what others have often said before me in this house, but if I emphasize the point it is because I realize the heavy responsibility weighing on the shoulders of every member of the house, and in particular, of every member of the government.
Such a sad state of affairs should not be allowed to last indefinitely. The time is past for groping policies or palliatives. The Canadian people are looking to us; in the last election, they entrusted us with a duty to fulfill, a duty which calls for firm action on our part. This reminds me of the words of a great philosopher and saint: "In order to remain honest and to be virtuous man must enjoy a certain degree of comfort and con-

tentment. . ." Then, how can one refrain from anxiety and alarm at the sight of the large number of unfortunate people who are denied even the necessaries of life.
Mr. Speaker, only a few months ago, I was simply a village stationmaster. When I was about to enter the political arena, my employer-who incidentally is well known by the right honourable Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King)-intimated that I had to choose between my position and politics. I am the father of six children, but I chose what I deemed to be my duty. I was dismissed, and had I not been elected in my constituency, I would now be one of the unemployed.
I have always led the simple life of the common people, whose hardships and whose sentiments I know well. I know that, even now as I am speaking, thousands of my constituents are suffering in silence and expecting this government to do something to alleviate the distress they have suffered too long. I feel that I would be remiss in my duty, that I would be neglecting to fulfill the mandate entrusted to me by my electors if I did not call the government's attention to the sad plight of my constituency.
The population which it is my privilege to represent in this house is largely made up of farmers, settlers, fishermen and workmen. Their distress is worse than is generally believed. Direct relief is practically non existent there; the municipalities being too poor to bear the cost of relief, the destitute must be content with public charity.
Numerous farmers, after clearing their lands and toiling arduously in the hope of leaving their farm some day to their children and peacefully ending their days with them are now threatened with bankruptcy. Farm produce, which in recent years was abundant, could not find a market. Potatoes have sold as low as 8 or 10 cents a bushel, And yet, this was the commodity on which the farmer depended to pay his taxes and his chief expenses. This year, prices are slightly higher, but the crop is short.
Many farmers have applied to the Canadian Farm Loan Board for a loan that might have saved them from ruin, but in nearly every case, the application was refused without any valid reason. I know that in many cases the applicant was too much of a Liberal in the eyes of the appraiser who himself happened to be a staunch Tory, However to-day, with the board constituted as it is, I am confident that they will be actuated by fairness rather than by political considerations.

Employment Commission-Mr. Lapointe (Matane)
Conditions among our workers, are not any brighter. Lumbering is the main industry in my constituency. In too many cases the men are at the mercy of their employers. I could cite a number of instances. Before action was taken by the provincial government, these unfortunate people had to toil from five o'clock in the morning to seven in the evening at a most arduous task for wages ranging from 40 cents to 80 cents a day.
Although conditions fiave somewhat improved since, they are still far from satisfactory. The employees of a certain sawmill, having made an attempt at organizing themselves into a trade union, were dismissed. I admit that they were reinstated, but the result was that such action dampened their enthusiasm and caused them to be on their guard. Well, Mr. Speaker, I must protest, with all my might, against such methods on the part of employers who, taking advantage of the distress prevailing among their men, are dealing with them in a most unfair manner and assuming the part of dictators.
I also wish to taire the opportunity, in my first address to this house, to register my protest against high salaries. At a time when so many people are starving, at a time when distress prevails in so many homes, I can scarcely conceive why some companies should pay to their favoured officials salaries altogether out of proportion with the meagre wages paid to their lower employees. I can still less imagine why employers should reduce the wages of their men in order to make it possible to pay fabulous salaries to themselves. Such tactics can only result in creating discontent and hatred among the working classes and paving the way to communism in this country.
I have no intention whatever of discussing communism in the course of this address; I simply wish to draw the attention of the government to the vile campaign carried on by the communists in this country. I know that the main objective of that campaign is to make this country a godless one. I shall have an opportunity of referring again to that question of communism, possibly in the course of the present session.
It being the duty of the state to extend equal protection to all classes of the population, I feel confident that our governments, both federal and provincial, will take the necessary steps to suppress such injustices practiced against our workers.
I also wish to join with those speakers who drew the attention of the government to the serious problem of youth, of our eager and vigourous young people who seek the opportunity to put their energy to work, but must perforce remain inactive. They lose all hope
as they see the best years of their life wasted away, years which they had intended to be so fruitful in achievement.
If I may be permitted, I shall submit to the government a suggestion which, if adopted, would largely solve the unemployment problem, especially in connection with the youth of my district. I have in mind the opening up to colonization of the vast plateau in the Gaspe peninsula, covering an area of over 10,000 square miles. Not only is it rich in minerals, but it is also covered with virgin forest and a soil of great richness. This splendid region is dotted with beautiful lakes and watered by magnificent rivers; in short it is a real paradise. Yet, the district is closed to settlement, owing to the lack of means of communication. The building of a railway was planned many years ago; why has the project not been carried out? The reason lies in the fact that it is intended to set that area aside as a reserve to be handed at a later date, as a gift to some outside concern which would hold our own people in a mercenary state while the best positions would go to their friends, as unfortunately it has been too often the case in our province.
Some may say that it is idle to think of building new railway lines, when the existing lines have become too great a burden. It may be so, but why? Too many lines have been built in certain districts and certain provinces and not enough in others. According to my information, had the province of Quebec been given the same consideration as was given to certain other provinces, it would now have over $500,000,000 worth of additional railway facilities. Therefore, I trust this government will not be deterred by a sense of false economy but will give their most serious consideration to the paramount question of developing the Gaspe region, the first soil trodden by the great discoverer, Jacques Cartier. This vast region only awaits the building of a railway to absorb the surplus of our population and the young people referred to a moment ago. Our young men would find there a splendid field of action in which to display their energy and put to useful work their strong arms which have remained so long inactive.
In my opinion, if the late government, instead of spending large sums of money in direct relief, wasting millions of dollars to no purpose, and spoiling our people in accustoming them to rely on the state for a livelihood, had undertaken such work as the building of the Gaspe railway, they would have achieved something useful and really worked in the best interest of the country.
1734	COMMONS
Employment Commission-Mr. Lapointe (Matane)
At a time when the back-to-the-land movement is advocated throughout the country as the best means of alleviating unemployment; when in Italy Mussolini has expended billions in draining marshes and irrigating vast plains in order to compel his people to take up farming and thereby solve to a large extent the unemployment problem, why should not our government, in cooperation with the provincial governments, shape their policy so as to facilitate a sound back-to-the-land movement. We cannot hope for an improvement of present conditions if we constantly apply the same remedies for the ills from which we are suffering. After having so long proclaimed that Canada is one of the world's richest countries in natural resources, the time has come, I think, to develop these vast and rich resources.
We are passing through a most tragic period. In spite of our unlimited resources, in spite of recent scientific discoveries, which could be so useful to us, our lot has never been worse. The reason is that we are living in an age of selfishness, conceit and envy, and I believe that so long as justice and Christian charity shall not have reassumed their proper place in the world, we cannot expect order, peace and happiness to reign.
In concluding, Sir, may I state that I have full confidence in the Liberal party. I firmly believe in the sense of fairness and justice of its leaders; I have great faith in the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) who, I know, is endowed with the great qualities that make for real statesmanship. The other day, as he was conversing with me in a simple and friendly way, I could not but feel impressed. It recalled to my mind certain incidents in my last electoral campaign, which was perhaps one of the most hardest and worst contests waged in the country, considering my meagre resources as compared with those of my opponents, and at the same time I could hardly help being amused when recalling some of their statements. "What can you expect a little fellow like Lapointe to do in parliament at Ottawa? He surely would be relegated in some corner I" Well, why did I come to this parliament? I came here to discharge my duty and serve my country to the best of my ability. Instead of being relegated in an out-of-the-way place, I was given a seat close to you, Mr. Speaker, while at my side, sir, two gallant soldiers who defeated two ministers in the last electoral contest. I wish to thank sincerely those to whom I owe such an honour.

In closing my remarks, I also wish to express my appreciation to this house for the kind attention and sympathy extended to a recruit undergoing his baptism of fire.
Mr. NORMAN J. M. LOCKHART (Lincoln) : Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention tonight to deal at length with the bill before the house, but I do desire to make a few specific references. I believe there is no necessity to go into statistical detail so ably covered this afternoon by the hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer). In a comprehensive manner he reviewed the statistical effect that the unemployment condition has had on Canada as a nation. Hon. members will recall that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) tabled information which should convince the house of the necessity for the government to deal with the relief situation in a most effective manner.
A few days ago considerable time was spent reviewing subsidies granted steamship companies on the Pacific coast. All hon. members listened with interest to the careful and comprehensive review of the situation. Large sums of money were awarded, and the matter was dealt with effectively. Then we passed on to a discussion of legislation providing ways and means to assist western wheat producers and to stabilize prices for the 1930 crop. Again millions of dollars were involved, and possibly for a very good cause.
To-day, however, we pass on to a definite consideration of something which in my opinion is vastly more important than a discussion of any o<f our basic commodities. To-day more or less we are bartering the lives of those Canadian citizens who have helped Canada become what she is to-day. We have before us a vague bill which has for its purpose the setting up of a national employment commission, a worthy purpose were it not for the dire necessity facing Canadian people at the present time. What is the commission to do? It is further to review what is to be done to preserve the lives and ideals of Canadian citizens.
May I refer briefly to a situation which developed in Canada during the regime of the Liberal party when it held office prior to 1930. During that time there developed one of the greatest financial crashes Canada has ever experienced; we all remember the effects of it. Out of those days came many serious complications. Hon. members who sat in the government of that day must be fully cognizant of all the circumstances leading up to that time. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was then in office, and

Employment Commission-Mr. Lockhart
had much to do with events that led up to that calamity. Following 1930 the Liberal party were in opposition for five years, and during that period observed and criticized the efforts of the Conservative government of that day. During that time they must have kept pace with all the trying conditions that the Conservative government was faced with during the five years it held office. The Liberal opposition must have observed that there was a slow but apparent improvement in general economic conditions in Canada.
Then, last October the Liberal party was again swept into power. Those of us who were engaged in the campaign do not forget the many slogans displayed throughout the length and breadth of the land, and on more than one occasion reference has been made to them in this chamber. We remember one which read:	"Vote Liberal and- do away
with unemployment." Surely the Liberal party w'ere sincere when they invited the Canadian people to support their claims to end unemployment. I want to refer particularly to one or two groups of Canadians to whom this appeal was made. It was made to a vast number of our middle-aged and older Canadian citizens, with many of whom I had personal contact. No doubt other hon. members experienced this same contact with people who were in dire difficulties. We saw the younger men and women who, as their positions became increasingly alarming, became desperate. They were disillusioned by the promise made by the Liberal party and they now find their problems are to be referred to a commission with powers to investigate.
