speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few remarks to make on this bill if they have not been contaminated or coordinated by the remarks of the previous speaker (Mr. Woodsworth).
I listened with great interest and admiration to the address of the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) when he was explaining this bill at considerable length. Obviously his speech was based upon a very careful study of the problem that confronts him and this country. He showed that he is a man well qualified to deal with this problem which he and his party in the election campaign described, and quite correctly, as the major problem of Canlada, and the question that occurs to me, and to which I have heard no satisfactory answers, is: Why does he not proceed to deal with it? I do not think it can be because he lacks confidence in his own Department otf Labour, because anyone who is familiar with its operations and has had the privilege of working with its .officials will, I think, agree with me that they are a fully qualified and zealous body of men. They are at his beck and call. Their training and the facilities of the department are at his disposal. They are already costing this country

considerable sums of money, and I wonder why the minister does not avail himself of that department which was put there for dealing with just the sort of problem that we are asked to deal with here, instead of appointing a commission of seven men, who will all have to be paid, and who will gather around them a staff which will also have to be paid. I am sure it is not because the Minister of Labour lacks confidence in his leader, because his leader is one, who, on his own showing, has dealt with labour's problems in all of their phases; he has been deputy minister of labour, Minister of Labour, editor of the Labour Gazette, a pillar of the Rockefeller Foundation during the war, dealing with labour problems; so surely the Minister of Labour is not setting up this commission because he feels that he will not get the help and support that he should from his leader.
Can it be that he lacks confidence in the members of this house? My feeling is that those who have been elected by the votes of the people, sent down to this capital, housed in a particularly perfect office building with every facility to do good work, provided with stenographic service, messengers, and all the latest in the way of office equipment, have rertain duties to perform by way of earning the fairly substantial subsidy they draw down. And just exactly why they should be deprived of these duties and functions, and why these should be transferred to a non-elected irresponsible commission, is a question that occurs to me, and to which I have heard no sufficient answer.
I should like to refer quite briefly to some of the remarks of the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), because in my humble opinion the appointment of this commission and the vesting in this irresponsible non-elective body of the power to advise on the expenditure of large sums of public money are not consistent with various remarks of the Prime Minister in his statement follow-the election, wherein he said, among other things:	.
The Liberal party has placed its trust in the people. The people to-day have reciprocated that trust in abundant measure. It will not be betrayed.
I submit that the transferring of the major national problem of this country to a nonelective irresponsible commission is a betrayal of that trust of the people.

I say that government by commission is the negation of democracy. Later on, he says again:

You, Mr. Speaker, will know better than I that the Chief Justice of England, Lord Hewart of Bury, one of the greatest parliamentarians and jurists in the world, has been carrying on for the past several years an intensive and successful warfare against government by commission. Furthermore, you will remember that the cudgels which he has been wielding so effectually on the heads of commissioners great and small have been taken up in this province and wielded with his customary vigour by a very great Liberal, none other than Sir William Mulock. I want to place on record a few observations from a recent judgment of Sir William on the habit of commission government which is becoming increasingly and dangerously prevalent.

If my hon. friend would allow me, before he forgets the passage, may I just draw to his attention the one paragraph to which I refer. The paragraph I wish to direct to the attention of my hon. friend is this:
To-day's election discloses that the people share the view, which the Liberal party has all along maintained, that unemployment is Canada's most urgent national problem. It is an endorsation of the Liberal proposal to deal with this question by means of a representative national commission, and by policies which will serve to revive industry and trade.

speechtext:
Oh, Mr. Speaker, anybody with ears heard this objectionable commission heralded long before to-night. There is nothing new in that. To quote, as I say, from what Sir William Mulock said about the commission habit; he deals with it in these words:
The method is always to brush aside everything which we have iearnt, and known to be workable, and to appoint some commissioner and proceed thus:
(a)	Get legislation passed in skeleton form.
There is your Bill No. 14. If there ever was
a skeleton, that thing is it.
(b)	Fill up the gaps with his own rules, orders and regulations.
I say that when we get these seven commissioners and they get their seven sisters,
cousins and aunts and their seven friends, we shall have a cocoon of rules, orders and regulations that will stifle anything the unfortunate unemployed are trying to get.
(e) Make it difficult or impossible for parliament to check the said rules, orders or regulations.
That will be done, and soon.
(d)	Secure for them the force of statute.
That is heralded already in the bill.
(e)	Make his own decision final.
That is what a great Liberal thinks about the commission form of government, ^ and although I do not often fall into the habit of commending statements by Liberals, I want to say that I endorse those views heartily, and further, that any government, any minister of labour, any prime minister and any party that turns over this, our most important national problem, to a non-elected, non-repre-. sentative commission, should apply to the College of Heralds and get leave to put beneath their coat of arms the words, "Let George do it."

subsubtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOR NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, along with others who have spoken to-day I wish to extend my congratulations to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers). The address which he gave was impartial and had something of the objectivity of the social scientist. While there were many statements with which I did not agree, and many things left unsaid that I thought ought to have been said, I cannot but feel that speeches on this high plane in this house should be more frequent in the future, and would make for a much better form of government.
It has become a platitude in the house to talk about unemployment as Canada's most urgent national problem, just as it has become a platitude to talk about poverty in the midst of plenty and about unemployment in a world crying for labour. Yet these things are only platitudes because they are so glaringly true and because we find all about us evidences of the wreck that has been left in the wake of the economic crisis through which we are passing. Were unemployment confined only to this country we might face it more hopefully, but it is not. Unemployment has touched every one of the civilized nations or at least every one of the capitalist nations of the world in the last five or six years. It is a rather childish waste of time to go back and try to ascribe unemployment to this or that political party, to try to tie it up to this or that administration.
The actual facts are these: The economic debacle started in 1929 and the Liberal administration had been in power nine years. They were not capable of preventing the debacle, just as other governments in other
1754	COMMONS
Employment Commission-Mr. Douglas
parts of the world were unable to prevent it. The people of Canada turned to a Conservative administration who fought with the problem valiantly and at least aggressively, but at the end of five years the problem was still with us, and to-day, in 1936, it is with us yet. The extent of that problem can best be understood by reference to sessional paper 102, which gives unemployment statistics for Canada for the past year. These statistics are slightly involved and I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that you call it eleven o'clock.
